title: The Fed’s Next Chair Faces AI Uncertainty, Political Heat and Credit Risks
content: The Federal Reserve has just cut rates by 25 basis points into an economy it still expects to grow faster next year, raising questions about why it eased and how much further it can go. Former Council of Economic Advisers chair Glenn Hubbard discusses the decision, the neutral rate and why he doesn’t see much more room for rate cuts going into 2026. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Affordability a 2026 Concern: Amalgamated CEO
content: Priscilla Sims Brown, Amalgamated Bank CEO, says most people agree affordability is a major concern. She tells Romaine Bostick and Katie Greifeld on “The Close” that the bank is deeply engaged in its Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy program and that 40% of its lending is climate related. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Airline Azul Wins US Court Approval of Restructuring Plan
content: Brazilian airline Azul SA won US court permission to exit bankruptcy and implement a creditor-backed restructuring that trims debt and lines up new investment from United Airlines Holdings Inc. and American Airlines Group Inc.

title: Overall Spreads Remain Tight Even As Oracle Debt Risk Jumps
content: On "Bloomberg Real Yield", Maureen O'Connor, global head of high-grade debt syndicate at Wells Fargo Corporate & Investment Bank, and Amanda Lynam, head of macro credit research at BlackRock, talks with Matt Miller about credit spreads, issuance and risks tied to the boom in AI growth. There’s a frenzy of development going on to support the AI revolution, and with it an insatiable demand for debt to fund it. Some estimate the overall infrastructure roll-out cost could reach $10 trillion, and with so many lenders lining up to throw cash at the assets, the fear is a bubble is building. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Clearlake-Backed Newfold Puts Side Deals at the Forefront in Debt Overhaul

title: Wall Street Week | Hubbard on Fed Cut Fallout, Open Source AI, Nuclear Bet, Department Store Revival
content: This week, Glenn Hubbard warns that tariffs, shaky data and a mature credit cycle create risks as the Fed looks toward 2026. And, will open AI ecosystems win out over closed models, as AMD CEO Lisa Su and former IBM CEO Sam Palmisano suggest? Plus, from AI to manufacturing, soaring electricity demand is forcing a rethink of where our power comes from and how fast we can build to generate it. Later, can Macy’s reinvent the department store for today’s shopper? (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Apollo Took Bets Against Software Makers Vulnerable to AI: FT

Shareholder voting It is approximately true that corporations are owned by their shareholders. [1] The managers of the company work for the shareholders, and the shareholders have the ultimate power to hire and fire them and to approve major strategic decisions. In practice, modern public corporations are owned mostly by diversified shareholders who are rationally apathetic<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/KBF7jGLyDol3L3W8eVSvHiE76P5e-jt0hirXK-RMRHWcrjheeEV3_GtWFtZAVxKvKZXGSM16_gMNHrvkqgLTDUZ-ZYsXHp1tmmK91MNku8eB0f3j2_rptOYawFa62DF6BOxPQqlRl98mqF1bkQ9L_MR9FdGmcHOcapJuDCypF1y-PGEzKQDlGc44rg4ygP8g_LmlDhiigLb0ip4BviWaED6HGS6e5LAQbEv5KWDMEG8qPlanWRaMdA2ueuFiT_xiLnS21k6FTGXvzecP4Eo2iYkwyUg3rkHiGmdmcUPetnVjAeW4-3l1m_QHDVEYOK-VStwkvS6vcFfBYlmv8kcwlcG6WUkZI4q6epwgNEzUTU58nVyTM-gGmfK3AA/GCebbGLUuXrGv75BBXGvRiw8L4TjDW-p/14>. If you have $1 million of retirement savings in the S&P 500 index, it would be absolutely insane<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/-uFa2N5etWvBVXF_zO2rc5wCeXG6pmfIMETwUZIuj9Yn9HOTttagOgLD2Wai4QrRq_5yLIhpe0Mbzd_ygGCm-l60aWog8M3nsrV0_OxrW9Z0CkwG0L0xrQind9qXnaTRQT_JlweVc8Uv07gcpjWeLSInUkb2rAh2VZx2L6ExCYo1N3R7g4AJiVOwpA9RbIrvrZ96ZyuikeXwD3rjNT3V4EPwXYJeSd6Es2rOjLZPRqagFxtCKGoHQnHgi0o2hZBB7kmJ3uVtTos5oox81_vge5iLnN4JeHwuy_oze2zbXF1ywRm9GnjzA0A7kVpZ4LKq3jdFnBgW3BwrJfWv4Slwtf8jg_mZtwlbDClOvS1y-0DxTVpgufFoxHFmSg/m2PPS1pKA3CPkdv4x4gnB6tbXRudKDkA/14> for you to spend even five minutes thinking about who should be the chief executive officer of Sealed Air Corp., or how much he should be paid, or what Sealed Airs strategy should be, or what Sealed Air does. Sealed Air represents about 0.016% of your portfolio, so its effect on your well-being is pretty small, and there are 499 other stocks in that portfolio, so you cant pay attention to all of them. And you own about 0.000003% of Sealed Airs stock, so your opinion about anything cannot possibly matter to Sealed Air. [2] Your best bet, with respect to oversight of Sealed Airs management and strategy, is to ignore it completely. On the other hand Sealed Airs managers cant just run around enriching themselves and ignoring shareholders. There has to be some oversight. It just has to be delegated: The shareholders have to get someone else to oversee the company for them, so they dont have to think about it. And this delegation also has to be pretty thoughtless and automatic: It would be insane for you to spend five minutes thinking about who you should hire to oversee Sealed Air for you. There are roughly three mechanisms for this, three sets of people to whom shareholders delegate their power over public companies: 1. Boards of directors. This is the oldest and most important answer. The board of the company is responsible for the management and oversight of the company. It hires and fires the CEO and makes the strategic decisions, sometimes asking shareholders to vote to ratify them. The board is nominally elected by the shareholders, but in almost every case directors run unopposed: In practice, the board chooses itself, with the current directors deciding whom to add to the board. [3] Why should you trust the board to oversee the company for you? Well, they do have fiduciary duties to look out for you, and if they do a bad job you can sue them. [4] They tend to get paid for their board service in company stock, so they are shareholders themselves and will want to look out for shareholders interests. Also, just, one has to assume a certain level of general professionalism in corporate life. These people devote at least several hours a quarter to serving on the board [5] ; they go to meetings and talk to managers; they have impressive resumes and professional reputations and want to be seen doing a good job. The directors understand that their job is to supervise the company on behalf of the shareholders, and mostly they try hard to do that well. 2. Professional investment managers. Above, I suggested that if you invest your retirement portfolio in the S&P 500, you are a shareholder of Sealed Air (an S&P 500 company), but probably you arent, at least not directly. Probably if you have $1 million in the S&P 500, its in an index-tracking mutual fund or exchange-traded fund managed by BlackRock Inc. or Vanguard Group or State Street Corp. or another professional asset manager. You delegate the whole problem of picking stocks, buying stocks and supervising the companies to the managers of your fund. If BlackRock wants to buy Sealed Air stock for you, it will. [6] If BlackRock wants to vote to approve Sealed Airs executive compensation on your behalf, it will. You dont care, and shouldnt. BlackRock is run by professionals who do this for a living, and you pay them to do it so you dont have to. And they too want to do a good job, both for general professionalism reasons and also to keep you as a paying customer. And part of their job is meeting with the managers of the companies and making sure that those managers are doing a good job. 3. Proxy advisory services. BlackRock is gigantic, and it has enough people and money to spend at least five minutes a year thinking about whether to approve Sealed Airs executive compensation. (Often at big managers these people will work in a separate governance department responsible for thinking about these things, while the portfolio managers who actually pick the stocks will not worry about voting.) But lots of professional investment managers have only billions of dollars under management, not trillions, and it is not necessarily rational for them to put that kind of time into thinking about the Sealed Air compensation vote. Sealed Air might be 0.1% of their portfolio, and they might own 0.003% of its stock instead of 0.000003%, but thats still not enough for their vote to make a difference to Sealed Air or to their returns. They cant, for regulatory and fiduciary-duty and shame reasons, simply throw the Sealed Air proxy statement in the garbage. But they cant, for good sensible time management reasons, read it either. So they outsource this thinking to a proxy advisory service  the big ones are Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis  that does this professionally. ISS and Glass Lewis will skim the Sealed Air proxy and be like sure vote for the comp package and many investment managers will just do what they say. None of these mechanisms is perfect, and the central point I want to make here is that they dont have to be because the shareholders dont have that much reason to care. People do complain, though. The imperfections are obvious: * The board might get a bit lazy. The directors will tend to be buddies with management, they are often former public-company CEOs themselves, and they might identify more with the managers than with the shareholders. If the CEO is doing a mediocre job, they might be inclined to say ehh good enough lets double her salary, while a zealous shareholder representative might fire her. * The professional investment managers and proxy advisory services might have their own professional biases. For one thing they probably live in New York or Boston and might have different cultural values from other shareholders. And if they have made corporate governance their lifes work, they probably care more about the formalities and norms of corporate governance than the average shareholder would. It is empirically the case<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/6pwPQn4T2fuQccWJAZcmPThbtkbIF-2gMtaa3Cs42Juk7i6OyVGvJxu4EjTbVL9MIx5m6PrQY_FWhJso_abS6e9TzR6iKBcc7HRWT8JbgV5YcZdPuygITLypGsKHA1xVLquMQrt5OLfJ3V28tI8zOU8_LP9_ic1EMT2_IuSWD8EjSgzOJNmyBzJcYlQpcAGJwAbOUt2G-V8sKgEJJ2vQtDe7PCHAEvgcCfrcWkjsXRXBfbj-Bygy3oDp1GB83kA0y02Ei0EaL1r5xP-cLUFsf2dtuGMytagHmKaWDu-0Cvu4H7K34XUO5EqD_QJEP1We85crQE5kcuZDYwmtEK3YBum-baodKoT9fpNegbGNgfZdem6H2SiVbKBHivk/jLcyzS-V-gfR9Ca4V-8h0gcSRbkd4xGt/14> that (1) a majority of Tesla Inc. shareholders would like to pay Elon Musk $1 trillion to build robots but (2) ISS and Glass Lewis disagree. Paying a CEO $1 trillion sounds cool to the average Tesla shareholder, but sounds distasteful to someone who has made a career of trying to exercise oversight over CEOs. Also, the shareholder advisers, unlike corporate managers and directors, generally dont have skin in the game: They dont get richer if the stock goes up, so they might vote for policies that they personally like even if theyre bad for the bottom line. [7] This stuff has become a culture-war issue, in part because it genuinely intersects with culture-war controversies  sometimes shareholders will be asked to vote on environmental or social proposals, and proxy advisers will have to take a politically charged position  and in part because CEOs tend to dislike interference from shareholders and so use culture-war rhetoric as a way to limit shareholder power. It is broadly though not always accurately assumed that professional investment managers and proxy advisers are relatively woke and left-wing, and so limiting their power  and putting more power in the hands of the board  is the right-wing move. And so in Donald Trumps presidency there have been efforts to shift power to boards of directors. We talked about the Securities and Exchange Commissions guidance cracking down on shareholder proposals<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/USDPvL1cEN39curNn_Nqt28UR4I3XZJWNEiW5GmF97c4TBgqn05CGb-kgx1xXIG8V5VCE-asXU2nOyq47D3LzeiHNbXeywkAv1wd1P8kT2qlMPLf8LeUiNp5zkpAYePZz0c5i0Oc40tW6_9v_fxYl70O5-yX0k270WRt5IvOMkDM3LSsg7EQwAgWWoVaTt5UohIIvWYSvH9hm21yXZmidnK7nIBzo2mbNxs8tES6gZnk4A_mXyBjvAJORPkJ8bvCda9jHbeAFAMI90WXa4Z-9CVu9dXmt1tnlmxZS9c2sNvbWT5JeGKdwXoj7VhKloROkuPQOB33CLQNKpgwAKkVukBBTluqdPLjAIM3Rdj2MMRltD_uj9zfCsilgoo/2ofEjuWSH9acvccnG8q4mRPDQrYQpndN/14>, because those proposals tend to give more power to investment managers and proxy advisers. And in September, Exxon Mobil Corp., with the SECs approval, achieved the dream of every public company: It launched a program in which retail shareholders can delegate their votes to the board<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/BgrUaQMrqDYkHBT9jvOzBFQaR3HhmHcRUX86CyX9fc8CY0LqaNWWQQSRTYXLczv6DrN9C6c0N6Ilvy7NGdyakG-x1ubP5ZsHKe6J2l3K21gMB_h6LNaDk1O_2HT3wf1CZJqamGOcX0USripWa-pDQSMIgJU_4Hv7yC8vM9b-0LXQ_4O90zcLEw7rhCp7sAxEr_2vim_lN4E9DCJYXME6nkGgwbhRcB-2acW3uUyOnF8GSTpFiQaISMPJs1vP6ABKEkUWSXpI2jtGHQ4X3fhSGQDjuQuHkB2-Xm-sXYz28v94pLZ32e94YUZWS4IZVKUsCsj11gI8xi8piUf3WfZe_jqipXNRq3NurjaArQhSXDUC25YrLKo9x_-QpFo/e_QB3oIMBFApDCHPv_LOTWFDoCHvoVrl/14>. Exxon said<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/atIsIcUpJiY8T1h0_sL16XQ3n4ZW2q_gjltWW4vahyOIB0SQa7ZkrFWj-tjaCWiM69LvR-6VEZXcORLgmFObXPpYjsgYFQvjsmbUSstEbGklRrNEtMyiGj948Wgt8mxq80SLtbxvBydNIrkMMDrCYc9pmBCsgj3MRzQJCHusz0N_zaiQmWsfgoVRnTOJO7C45wtkDkfqCwDoOuONv_2WtoeCyhzlUuacW-qSdBdRf2LqIF9mRTa08o5wiBIo7C-329JjjsOsBOaa7uksDbIz13yXt0Qf0CkJidM8zG8L44H9WpAoHwntuLeI2CfIigTwG8-EyPNMM-1uyrfVNRfLmrLS4RlQVhvMhXdJHYL-MPw0zP64nMpY5-vqygg/Us12lsGeELAb39GKW2KyBoGPM_YoNkK2/14>: ExxonMobils retail investors, many of whom are retired and depend on ExxonMobils dividends to support their livelihoods, have voiced significant frustration over the annual time commitment required to vote at our meetings of shareholders. Each year, retail investors face a large number of proposals to vote on. This burden is not just a matter of hours spent; it also disproportionately impacts retail investors who lack access to professionals dedicated to voting. This limits their participation in shareholder democracy. Yes, it is insane to participate in shareholder democracy, and now they dont have to. Of course they didnt have to before: In practice, retail shareholders mostly didnt vote, which meant that the votes of professional investment managers and proxy advisers carried more weight. Now the retail shareholders can automatically vote with the board, somewhat diluting those professional votes. But for most companies the real prize is not to get retail shareholders to go along with whatever the board wants, but to get index funds to go along with whatever the board wants. Today the Wall Street Journal reports<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/95YzZzvjvz5yCELqsP-R0918tASLpelr4yHxYeEsBtIiAnzfr8bUjtODJ79VkKH294m20tbmkEBUA0K1qm5aKHj9BV4QCeDqAT4WQercgsVXk1utrGJ5i8lHyh1C1WWoHNmPhLSpNib51jzjfI-3AMKc6wYayWIfzu-TzCYPzPnWKPO3yPw3FXr8m2fCV3K-d--vXvSXHjihHVZ9TiQ52sIrjYPDzoIcThgqLIB1fT4c4WHD19f7LspMQgn1hKoXrShXMOsr7OkQrm-qhS_BExmsc6uOpQIAKwKKll3daL8a1zQ7OHXMreYA0iblZBAbwpmOzcLkg1mzOMbf63R2mUElPUOdyhvCVl2xrVTQOvsfA3Vz3tWznplMnzQ/WDrdbML93-IsrKV91jswUSBQNr-Xj1tT/14>: The White House is exploring new measures to curb the influence of proxy advisers and index-fund managers, wading into a hot-button debate raised by high-profile CEOs including Elon Musk and Jamie Dimon in recent months. Trump administration officials are discussing at least one executive order that would restrict proxy-advisory firms such as Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis, people familiar with the matter said. That could include a broad ban on shareholder recommendations or an order blocking recommendations on companies that have engaged proxy advisers for consulting work, the people said. Officials also are exploring limits on how index-fund managers are allowed to vote, seeking to curtail the power of such behemoths as BlackRock, Vanguard Group and State Street, the people said. These three together own on behalf of clients roughly 30% or more of many of the biggest U.S. publicly traded companies. One measure being discussed would require these index-fund managers to mirror their votes in line with clients who choose to vote. ISS and Glass Lewis provide recommendations to asset managers on how to vote on shareholder ballots on topics ranging from executive pay packages to environmental goals. Musk recently lashed out at the firms when they recommended a no vote on his historic $1 trillion pay package. Tesla shareholders approved the plan last week. From first principles it really is obvious that direct and indirect shareholders of public companies should outsource most of their voting decisions to specialized professionals: Individual shareholder votes basically dont matter. But if they do all outsource their voting to the same professionals, then those aggregated votes do matter, at least sometimes, at least symbolically. (Musk got his money!) And so there will be fights over who gets to make the voting decisions, and what decisions they should make. Total portfolio approach One of the great intellectual discoveries of modern finance is that, for many purposes, you can treat every stock as a combination of statistical factors. The traditional way to think about a stock is to analyze the companys financial statements, sample its products, talk to its customers, meet with the chief executive officer to evaluate her handshake firmness, and form a view on its prospects and valuation. And then if the stock goes up, you will explain that with reasons like sales of the new product were strong or the CEO was able to cut marketing costs without affecting sales or some other company-specific narrative reason. And then there is the modern factor approach where you analyze a stock by saying, like, it tends to go up when value stocks go up, and when small-cap stocks go up, and its coefficient on the value factor is X, and its coefficient on the size factor is Y, and its coefficient on the CEO handshakefulness factor is Z, and so on down the line, decomposing each stock into its historical correlation to various statistical factors and themes. I mean, you dont analyze the stock like that; your computer does. Your computer regresses all the stocks against some sensible list of factors. And then if the stock goes up, you will explain that with reasons like the value factor outperformed today or whatever, some statistical market-wide set of stories. There are all sorts of uses and implications of this in the stock market. Quant hedge funds are doing some form of this, analyzing thousands of stocks to figure out their common drivers and then betting that some drivers will do well. Smart beta funds do versions of this cheaply and at scale, and big multistrategy hedge funds track their factor exposures to make sure that their portfolio managers are not just picking factors: To earn your keep as a modern fundamental equity portfolio manager, you cant just make a big bet on the value factor; you have to add some idiosyncratic insight. But a growing list of funds is challenging that convention by turning to a method that ditches the asset-class silos. Instead, they pit investments as disparate as, say, public equities and private credit against each other in search of the best bet for the whole portfolio. Dubbed the Total Portfolio Approach, its gaining traction fast  and before month-end it may even be the guiding principle of Americas largest public pension. For many such allocators, adopting TPA will mean making drastic changes in culture, governance and infrastructure. Meanwhile there are plenty of skeptics who see little more than a buzzy acronym. But to its proponents, TPA is a better fit than the old static model  known as Strategic Asset Allocation  for an unpredictable world where the likes of inflation spikes or geopolitical shocks can easily upend market assumptions. In the platonic ideal of TPA, a board would trust the investment team to make more ad hoc decisions. Staff would freely share information across asset-class teams and would debate whether they should bet on, say, data centers through listed shares or private loans. Quants would dissect the factor exposures of public and private equity alike. The passive benchmarks that previously loomed over every asset class team would be no more. If, for example, a PE allocation has risen to 20% from a target of 15%, an SAA investor might be compelled to offload some PE holdings even if liquidity constraints mean pricing is unfavorable. But a TPA fund can cut listed shares instead, since the framework views both as equities driven by similar forces. It seems obviously true that private equity and public equity are related bets that should in some sense be substitutes for each other, but as a practical matter historically those have been different asset classes managed and overseen by different people, and it was hard to opportunistically move between them. But if they are all just statistical correlations then you might as well try. Their holdings of US equities have nearly doubled this year to a record $170bn at the end of October, according to Korea Securities Depository data. Many have been drawn to the resurgence in meme stocks this year, helping fuel a craze that first took hold during the Covid-19 pandemic. Korean retailers are just crazy. They are not like average retail investors in other parts of the world. They are very aggressive, said Jongmin Shim, Korea equity strategist at CLSA. Chung Ji-eun uses a local brokerages mobile trading system and often sacrifices sleep to trade US stocks for about two hours from midnight Korea time because of the 14-hour time difference. It is so easy to buy and sell US stocks in the system. title: FW: 13/11/25: Alle Augen auf die PBB, Sparkassen-Fusion, Apobank plant Debt-Fonds
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene - Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Thursday, 13 November 2025 06:19:19 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 13/11/25: Alle Augen auf die PBB, Sparkassen-Fusion, Apobank plant Debt-Fonds Außerdem: Wieso operationelle Risiken für Banken neu klassifiziert werden müssen [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/69fd6614-b124-afd1-a646-f535755d8bf5.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=ff5bdf2631&e=8f69674dd2> Geht's bei der PBB schon wieder um alles? Unser Live-Blog zu den Q3-Zahlen Was genau ist eigentlich das Problem der Deutschen Pfandbriefbank? Schon klar, als nach der Zinswende der gewerbliche Immobilienmarkt crashte, da gerieten nahezu alle Hypothekenbanken in eine gewisse Verlegenheit. So richtig ins Straucheln kam aber nur eine, nämlich die PBB (siehe im Februar 2024 unser Deep Dive -> Steht die Deutsche Pfandbriefbank wirklich vorm Kollaps?<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=1f0730d05b&e=8f69674dd2>). Und als sich die Risikoergebnisse und damit die Gewinne zuletzt wieder zu stabilisieren begannen (siehe -> Die beste Performance seit langem: Hypothekenbanken lassen Krise hinter sich<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=516350d1af&e=8f69674dd2>) - da war bei einem Player von alldem nichts zu sehen. Nämlich bei der Deutschen Pfandbriefbank. Quasi: Geht's allen Immobanken schlecht, dann geht's der PBB besonders schlecht; und geht's allen Immobanken wieder besser, dann geht's der PBB trotzdem weiter schlecht. Wobei ein bisschen diffus bleibt, warum das so ist. Jedenfalls: Auch dieser Tage hängt über der Deutschen Pfandbriefbank also wieder dieses "Was läuft da eigentlich immer schief?"-Gefühl. Weil Anfang November plötzlich die Aktie crashte. Und sich hinterher herausstellte, dass es vorher sogenannte Pre-Calls mit Analysten gegeben hatte - wobei die bei diesen Gesprächen vermittelten Vibes offenbar nicht die allerbesten waren. Was steckt wirklich dahinter? Gab's im dritten Quartal lediglich einen kleinen Dip, auf den man die Analysten vorbereiten wollte? Oder kracht es schon wieder so richtig im Gebälk? Unser Live-Blog zu den Q-Zahlen kennt die Antwort. Und zwar bis ungefähr 7.50 Uhr. FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=f964dc65bb&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/47c2c8e0-6acb-44b4-ad35-f59b8513040e.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c5a04d1864&e=8f69674dd2> Jetzt noch Steuervorteile für 2025 sichern! Mit dem ETF Rürup von Raisin investieren Sie breit gestreut und kostengünstig in Aktien- und Anleihen-ETFs und können in 2025 bis zu 29.344 € steuerlich geltend machen. Für Ehepaare gilt der doppelte Betrag. Wenn Sie sich den Steuervorteil für 2025 noch sichern wollen, muss das Produkt bis zum 12. Dezember 2025 abgeschlossen werden. Jetzt sichern.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=21aa963674&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Exklusiv: Apobank will eigenen Debt-Fonds auflegen - bis zu 750 Mio. Euro Volumen: Als nächstes hiesiges Geldinstitut nach Playern wie der Deutschen Bank, der Helaba oder Berenberg will nun auch die Apobank ins Geschäft mit Debt Funds vorstoßen. Laut Informationen von Finanz-Szene peilt das Düsseldorfer Spezialinstitut für sein erstes derartiges Vehikel ein Fondsvolumen zwischen 500 Mio. und 750 Mio. Euro an - der Zeichnungsschluss ist im ersten Halbjahr 2026 geplant ... ... Um das geplante Volumen stemmen zu können, tut sich die Apobank mit der Deutsche Credit Capital AG zusammen. Dabei handelt es sich um einen in Frankfurt ansässigen Finanzierungs-Spezialisten, der - gegründet 2017 - während Corona in die Insolvenz rutschte und nun im Zuge einer Kapitalerhöhung den Neustart wagt (als CEO firmiert Ex-IKB-Manager Nicolaus Loos, zum AR-Chef wurde kürzlich Credit-Suisse/Flatex-Veteran Martin Korbmacher ernannt, der einzige veröffentlichte Jahresabschluss ist sechs Jahre alt, an der Bafin-Zulassung wird gerade gearbeitet) ... ... Die Korbmacher-Truppe will die Mittel für den Fonds überwiegend bei institutionellen Investoren einwerben, darüber hinaus soll die Apobank ihre Wealth-Management-Klientel angehen. Auch bei der Kreditgenerierung (ein Debt-Fonds braucht schließlich Debt) ist das Heilberufler-Institut zumindest teilweise involviert. Dabei geht es um bonitätsschwächere Kunden, denen die Apobank wegen ihres Risikoprofils (und der damit verbundenen Kapitalbindung) kein eigenes Geld leihen will. Den größten Teil der Forderungen soll allerdings der Partner, also die Deutsche Credit Capital, reinholen. Ticker * Die Rede ist von einem "Dialog". Aber wenn nicht alles täuscht, dann dürfte daraus die nächste, gar nicht mal so kleine Fusion im roten Sektor werden. Founded in 2016, Einride has built a business model that blends its “freight-capacity-as-a-service” offering with a SaaS platform that provides the full ecosystem needed to run electric and autonomous operations. While the firm has faced some ups and downs - including substantial losses last year and layoffs - it's also enjoyed solid recurring revenue and won regulatory approvals across the US and Europe. With this move, Einride is positioning itself to scale in the US, where favourable regulatory dynamics and infrastructure could unlock the next chapter of transport innovation. But as the SPAC route remains a challenging path - especially for hardware-heavy, capital-intensive businesses - the stakes are high. November 2025 Der Tag Das Wichtigste aus der Wirtschaft ­ [https://cdn.prod.www.manager-magazin.de/images/d1cc8cca-49eb-4994-93f1-454bc8860ae6_w112_r1_fpx51_fpy46.jpg] Vinzenz Neumaier Redakteur manager magazin Lieber Herr Frignani. Brose-Patriarch Michael Stoschek (77) ist der Typ Unternehmer, den man getrost einen Macher nennen darf. Aus einem kleinen Mittelständler formte er einen Konzern mit mehr als 7 Milliarden Euro Umsatz. Bei Meinungsverschiedenheiten hat Stoschek immer gern das letzte Wort. Zwar wollte sich der Unternehmer eigentlich schon längst aus dem Operativen zurückziehen. Aber, man kennt es, die Sorge um das Lebenswerk ließ einen Ruhestand partout nicht zu. Stattdessen bleibt es auch nach fast 80 Lenzen dabei: Stoschek macht einfach immer weiter. Zu tun gibt es genug, denn bei Brose läuft es nicht rund. Zuletzt gab es sogar ein dickes Minus. Grund genug für den Brose-Granden, auf Partnersuche zu gehen. Kann vielleicht ein Zulieferer in Familienhand aus Indien in Franken aushelfen? Mein Kollege Christoph Seyerlein weiß: Wen Patriarch Michael Stoschek als Brose-Investor favorisiert (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf125db52510ff8e9756565f6418b21327a6661c3cf0301712d4fc58790156a0cd1d825b2a35762b92fa9f84370bbf30ca0e6b918b61a575da6c>. ANZEIGE [desktop] <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12aad5d3e7d23f1aa18dc5a1bf6f2dbb052e25494302e47ec167d54c9a71751f5dff1231625153f6deb9f2623d155e8da3cd61a81892f54e15> [mobile] <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12aad5d3e7d23f1aa18dc5a1bf6f2dbb052e25494302e47ec167d54c9a71751f5dff1231625153f6deb9f2623d155e8da3cd61a81892f54e15> [Was schert ihn sein Geschwätz von gestern: Brose-Oberhaupt Michael Stoschek] Was schert ihn sein Geschwätz von gestern: Brose-Oberhaupt Michael Stoschek Brose [separator] Die Wirtschaftsnews des Tages: * Thomas Coesfeld (35) setzt sich gegen seinen älteren Bruder Carsten Coesfeld (38) durch und wird Chef des milliardenschweren Medienkonzerns Bertelsmann. Die Entscheidung wurde lange vorbereitet  und markiert doch den Höhepunkt einer Karriere im Eiltempo (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12f1311047dd5973c56b1c1fc816ea269b8932f54a5888ea5aeeac85c8db6626d3786caaf4b93851e93b86698591e3a1170525b534bb07ec17>. * Klatsche vor dem Bundesgerichtshof: Wirecard-Aktionäre dürfen ihre Forderungen nicht wie normale Gläubiger im Insolvenzverfahren anmelden. Auch wenn die Eigenkapitalgeber getäuscht wurden, sind ihre Forderungen weiterhin nachrangig<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12c65b2a0610c73d2e434aa9f808a8e0c0e217d35895ddaf410dcac2d484b95b70f5a95f280cd71c8f37d97a90884f053e14aaecbeb7149c2a>. Das Geld ist damit ziemlich sicher futsch. * Des einen Pleite ist des anderen Erfolg. Während Konkurrent Starcar mit der Insolvenz kämpft, hat der Autovermieter Sixt im dritten Quartal weiter zugelegt und mehr verdient. Ausgelassen ist die Stimmung im Landkreis München aber trotzdem nicht  das Unternehmen reduziert seine Umsatzprognose für das Gesamtjahr<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12d6c3f39008e7559364b473e6961e498a3434f911e2f6910a781c038a2b672090db55cdbcd3394ffef2ec639a8615b592b9bdabf81ffdf297>. [separator] Was Sie beim Spülen interessieren könnte: * Offenbar bin ich nicht der einzige begeisterte Putzmann, der auf die Marke Frosch schwört. Meine werte Frau Mama hat die Hausflure immer mit den Öko-Mittelchen der Firma Werner & Mertz aus Mainz gereinigt. Ich tue es ihr nach  wenn auch nicht mit derselben Regelmäßigkeit. Reinhard Schneider (57) wird es freuen: Der Geschäftsführer von Werner & Mertz feiert Umsatzrekorde und zeigt der Konkurrenz, dass man auch mit Nachhaltigkeit frisch und erfolgreich sein kann. Der Preis dafür: Schneider wurde zum Entrepreneur des Jahres in der Kategorie Nachhaltigkeit gekürt<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12cf961ce3b93ea37e659912f4d1d13709d6e8213c0f58e866843a1aad403434cf65eb0ea259ab9c6de9428a047ddd33c0db7ad4bb0c6bdfff>. Zur Feier dieser Nachricht werde ich mit Froschs Anti-Kalkmittel heute Abend erst einmal gründlich meine Badewanne reinigen. Blackstone If you work in financial markets and are very smart and diligent, you might occasionally notice something weird. Some stock is trading at too high a price, or too low. Some company is being run inefficiently, and if you take it over you can make it worth more. Some company has violated the terms of its bonds<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/D8_L9LuKieiXAoxj_DDRS5Ot72axp37xK7VUgPQfopitqiQDuhPdnXMQ5BxdY5IRXkQwQO5qTFpTS5WBJnUTF8yOq8rIaJmbF1XjNYyYWC2Mwezj2Qcnx9JXIuKsaCIRP_5ivJa5I0PAEv-U9LifyV3-FrxubumjTnBGePjmSmzbYI19NahJ6UQSOxXRuV33mOAUevJUmnQYTxT1_6ZBG4rrxFj-Zs4wzmkMAWZkKYK20XzWlGKd4b9OVUTVdyzO4EbUmjwMLKaY6RYN56TCzFgCe6wOkvjB6ccmk-iVrmwVPnrc2sg_RgnYgSv3dl9pS25NDpsbkzDBHG0xnBzNVm-HunJBKju3x2E8wq9kzT4bNrUKdqBr2sRvJA/-DQ7wWUZtcih-8QlA5b0-4ksSFTyQ8Ms/14>, and if you buy up the bonds<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/mNGqOBTRgEzvb0F9hIB28vPwTVeqqbwbgfdYWp9rAOZilFOy_lQDIoRUw1_w8WpMPC4aXK9Z5tlLijUG6e0c6vj5Y_YS3mkGUuT6vFTCrXF12e0oF69CbzaJOkrVNurYHrnYCDULRqIJ1DqKQwQ_YIkcc8tdmMEIQuh_ZU5uYPPdqGj7DIlvcXSXMtrJiYBUP6j4ka_AFtvOp2gpwsvhJb8WRHtCZmFaeJ55vRaYHNbBXjwevqk0YyDBESQslvMf2iLCra3aXFIt_p1YwzgWem7hRq8QsVVo9zKJHieAR2M6qJDJiuRSOkGo8ct2AV_JNQztZQlpHkLxxbQtMqblBWbpn7tOsPPcRmYeI6azoSG4kHMDfVfVRKwqtA/gBItttlL78zuQyiFsIdZu4zZlkMRp_Fw/14> you can put the company into bankruptcy and extract a lot of value. Some asset is trading at a tiny discount to some economically equivalent asset, and if you buy one and sell the other and lever up the trade you can make some money. The Ruritanian stock market goes up on Tuesdays when it rains, so you should buy Ruritanian stocks on Monday afternoon when the forecast is for rain. All sorts of anomalies and dislocations and inefficiencies and opportunities. These opportunities have different scales. By some measures, one of the greatest of all trades is the reverse split arbitrage<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/MhzscDdG3TwyBanNBlkhVLPXgiWnIr1R1J_R9WMWpyBedmt72rmV1RcW4ksw9TECAfj4i56x0DHuFtmzSyUSl5JyHCh-6Z65GHuvz1EHq66Rxr2OAHhxJNe5XIM4IqRhn10nfzNyEgyy6E8KzLs0WPOfSG9LnkWNideXk0rjpLMs5_2CkOtmYbaprMHBIUPvwnZk2PJo13shvp-RdiJ6IBgx0UxCooKMGswpHFlf6F6ig0MtkIsgbwswBs-MlIgKjtpYm4x-0PFDNM2M0v_X_cdck8DEfzT5Fa8jSKcYeWmksA2P8JhTO4zWuzwIFYZhBb419c2ZPyNSwiV81VwX4c8iobYYEUpTa1c55VOhE6zfWLkfh9Kz4TsxpA/fIAGfklEf_m7z6RmRjRwBKomtjBN9nfw/14>: When a tiny company does a reverse stock split, it will often round up, so if you buy one share of a company as soon as it announces a 1-for-10 reverse split, you can end up with a quick and reasonably certain 900% return on your investment. But this only works with one share; you cannot in any sensible way scale it up. [1] You can make, like, $4.50 on a $0.50 investment: It is a true market anomaly that you can exploit, but not very much. Other trades have much bigger scales. Jane Street Group was able to extract perhaps a billion dollars from, uh, lets say noticing some anomalies<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/rARuaZ5Xo0D7Wp-Q-rL82Su6BdEIg1g4wri6YFFI0_V8tDhjsbIyW2Kh7qID1iy6HXaWWhaozvpeLw8F5vFDANVkAy59YGp5KZhoW1L93r2PuGXixcHlXvfIKAL0_-EoGEF4uohGkw3cR9rn0HD_uQK8ez6CEJPysGZEXQdaKVsrfOVHa5Sy1Iwp8O0QE0XrZ4aO3JK7kwuZHr_FhjObQNdW9UE-JYIVaB6Sq3q-oWI2dfyMkWY01YTx4B5UlqA3g4K_e6DEX7dgsLrioqTPv5TOjp0a6dN4NKV8cMvdHiU8zAqB-ePTbIWqkVr-jbqynN5JlMLugF2LvQ1n0uNwKYxK4QWQ2W1U048CNFYN2foRHB-Y3aiMXGWa2w/_W4ROa6Pg51IbhusFgfSLb2oSgn3JdbI/14> in the Indian options market. Renaissance Technologies has spent decades taking billions of dollars out of financial markets by noticing anomalies on an industrial scale. But there are tens of trillions of dollars in the financial markets. Jane Street and Renaissance are big in the sense that they have made billions of dollars for their executives, but in the scale of financial markets the anomalies they exploit are tiny. Somebody can make some money  billions of dollars  by finding weird inefficiencies in financial markets. But everybody cant make all the money that way. In the aggregate, financial markets are not a grand bet on market anomalies; that would make no sense. Everyone cant be noticing inefficiencies that no one else notices; everyone cant be taking money from everyone else by being cleverer than everyone else. In the aggregate, financial markets are a grand bet on global economic growth. People sometimes divide investing into alpha and beta. Alpha is, approximately, finding opportunities that no one else has noticed and making contrarian bets on them. Beta is, approximately, using your savings to buy a share of global economic growth. BlackRock Inc., the giant asset manager, has more than $13 trillion of assets under management<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/IF01v2zLxFZRyux-cCw4-LPOxcfA_1GAOgE-EKRl_qr9pSQ3tnZpHURO4NGdo3s_hr--ZJp2ECcTjq0yLZQ68PSNijGTP14bSPvjekkH2LWeihsQ7yTeIxeZMpoJ9VsaH601n6DOTEkIOFz_2NVoVZKtNlLHUPmSLTn8eSYG9ZaWsaW0Pk8mz1J9K-3TVzxeocZJFhkMpGAeyiug7NlxJDVT48WK1hAieJlarDSCP69e8ZVqFoZdWtzi-zLcfZscx_NDUE5b9vALTodb3EU-oXevMn10ZzTC_wFap0OGgSs8X1c5rLxycjyTLtu4bZfL1lJXJ2IQ3DiSn9PKfX51ZduegIkIcjMTfm6wr3xVL_v2gpuuLl80RlySv-c/n8GuPEXhu6UD1LnhmQrhCGcIDJ2-7ayg/14>, more than half of which is in index funds and exchange-traded funds. You do not put your money into a BlackRock S&P 500 index ETF because you hope BlackRock will spot clever anomalies. Youre just there for your cut of global economic growth. Many of the people who got rich and famous in financial markets did so by spotting anomalies. (That tends to work faster than global economic growth.) The most ambitious of them naturally want to scale up: run more money for more people to generate more returns and collect more fees for themselves. This is possible, at some scale. The biggest multimanager multistrategy pod shop hedge funds are essentially industrial anomaly factories: They compete fiercely to hire talented spotters of market inefficiencies, they deploy as much capital as they can against those opportunities, and they scale up by hiring more people to spot more uncorrelated anomalies. This opportunity  the market undervalues and underlevers companies, so we can borrow money to buy them ourselves and extract extra profits  turned out to be absolutely enormous. It turned out that you could do leveraged buyouts of companies worth tens of billions of dollars, and this business could support multiple big firms each with hundreds of billions of dollars under management. And those firms could, at least arguably, earn market-beating returns: They gave their investors not just the returns of allocating capital to economic growth, but also the bonus returns of spotting market inefficiencies and correcting them. Some veterans lamented that the swagger was gone and that investing felt akin to being in a factory or flipping burgers in a line. Yes: If you run trillions of dollars, you are going to invest in big themes like AI or India. Where can we get access to global economic growth, you will ask yourself, and you will answer with words like AI or India. If your answer is this company has particularly low-priced bonds so if we triggered its CDS with a manufactured default we could make a huge recovery, that is the wrong sort of answer; you are thinking too small. If your answer is we could put some more leverage on this $20 billion public company, even that is now too small. The right sort of answer is AI or India. Your themes have to be big. So like I want to buy Treasury bonds contingent on the Democrats winning the Senate in 2026 or whatever, a trade where (1) I get the asset if the event occurs, (2) the trade is unwound if the event does not occur but (3) in the interim, the conditional asset itself trades and has a price. One benefit of this is, you know, more ways to manage risk, more ways to speculate, etc. But another benefit is that the prices of the conditional assets could give you information about possible futures: not about how likely the event is, but rather what the effects of the event might be. The price of one barrel of oil contingent on invading Iraq could tell you something about (market expectations about) what invading Iraq would do to oil prices. After I wrote about shareholder voting yesterday, reader Charles Wang emailed to suggest: The obvious correct resolution for delegating shareholder votes is to have one publicly traded contract that is a forward contract for the stock conditional on the vote passing and another forward contract for the stock conditional on the vote failing. Really it's a bit bizarre that the markets are supposed to be about efficient allocation of capital but the one thing that's directly about allocation of capital is not settled by the markets. title: FW: 14/11/25: Herber Rückschlag für Neobroker, Kehrt bei N26 jetzt Ruhe ein?
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Friday, 14 November 2025 06:00:22 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 14/11/25: Herber Rückschlag für Neobroker, Kehrt bei N26 jetzt Ruhe ein? Außerdem: DKB, BayernLB, Deka, Aareal, PBB, OLB, Procredit, Union [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/e40e4f4a-9191-ea2c-acd1-889d7bf8f5ab.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=f050255224&e=8f69674dd2> Wochen-Podcast (KW 46) "Die PBB ist ein negativer Outlier  und diese Woche hat sie gezeigt, wieso" [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/fa91ed80-8389-ee20-7188-39989e72455f.png] Die Themen diesmal: #1: Die Pfandbriefbank vermittelt Investoren ein Gefühl, als seien nicht immer alle relevanten Informationen auf dem Tisch #2: Kosten im Griff, Ziele in Reichweite  die Aareal Bank ist mittlerweile in vielen Punkten das glatte Gegenteil der PBB #3: Die Deka mag viele Probleme haben  aber es gibt nicht viele Unternehmen, die sich solche Problem so locker leisten können #4: Bei der BayernLB entschwand von heute auf morgen die Risikochefin. Doch das Risikoergebnis  fällt ganz formidabel aus! #5: Bei der DKB fragt man sich Quartal für Quartal, wie lange sie ihr Ergebnisniveau noch halten kann. Aktueller Eindruck: noch lang! #6: Ein Sparkassen-Chef on air  wie wir auf die Geschichte vom überaus lukrativen Goldschatz der Kreissparkasse Biberach gekommen sind #7: Was die Entwicklung des Core-Bank-Spezialisten Mambu über den Werdegang hiesiger Fintech-Unicorns erzählt Auf geht's: Finanz-Szene (frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=106af4dbf9&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/1f355e5c-a37c-48c8-869a-69500bd0b72c.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=5ba4764732&e=8f69674dd2> AI Regulierung  sind Sie bereit? Der EU AI Act zwingt Banken zum Handeln. Wer AI gewinnbringend nutzen will, braucht Regeln, Transparenz und technische Souveränität. Das Whitepaper zeigt, wie es geht  Best Practices inklusive. Jetzt Zugriff sichern.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=89ec525515&e=8f69674dd2> Wie die PSD Bank München zur Mutter aller Zinswende-Verlierer wurde (frei zugänglich) Die Reihen sind eng bestuhlt und dicht besetzt, als die PSD Bank München Ende Juni in einem Innenraum der Augsburger Fußball-Arena ihre Generalversammlung abhält (die PSD Bank München sitzt nicht in München, sondern in Augsburg, darum veranstaltet sie dort auch ihre Mitgliedertreffen). Rund 350 Mitglieder sind angereist, wie im Mittelschiff einer Kirche hat man sie postiert, fünf Stühle rechts, fünf Stühle links, dazwischen nur ein schmaler Gang, kein halber Meter breit, so würde man anhand eines in Umlauf gebrachten Fotos schätzen. Vorne, am Altar, hocken derweil die Großkopferten, es sind mehr als sonst, denn wie die Mitglieder an diesem Abend erfahren werden, nimmt die PSD Bank München ein großflächiges Revirement ihrer Führungsebene vor. Karen Lehmann-Martin, vor fünf Jahren zur Vorstandschefin gekürt, wird sich zeitnah zurückziehen, "aus Altersgründen", wie es heißt, sie ist 61; auch der fürs Kreditgeschäft zuständige Vorstand Jürgen Haschka demissioniert. Stattdessen übernehmen Jens Fischer (bis April noch Chef der PSD Bank Hessen-Thüringen) und Timo Memmer, der von der VR Bank Südliche Weinstraße-Wasgau kommt und zunächst noch als Generalbevollmächtigter firmiert. Ganz schön viele Neuigkeiten also für die Mitglieder, aber das ist noch nicht alles, was sie an diesem Abend erfahren werden. Denn  auch der Jahresbericht liegt zur Lektüre bereit. Und, tja, was soll man sagen: Der hat es in sich! Und zwar in einer Art und Weise, wie es noch selten ein Geschäftsbericht eines deutschen Kreditinstituts in sich gehabt hat. Lesen Sie hier, wie es möglich ist, dass sich die Cost-Income-Ratio einer Bank binnen weniger Jahre von knapp 70% auf 199% (!!!) verschlechtert. Und warum das noch nicht einmal das einzige dramatische Problem der in Augsburg ansässigen Münchner ist  unsere exklusive Recherche aus dem Juli, jetzt für kurze Zeit vor der Paywall: Finanz-Szene (7 Tage frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=82e593e04e&e=8f69674dd2> Blog * Insbesondere Neobroker wie Trade Republic oder Scalable Capital hatten zum Start der Frühstart-Rente auf einen regelrechten Booster-Effekt gehofft. Nun kommt zum Leidwesen der Fintech-Branche alles doch ein bisschen anders. Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=0eb80f5507&e=8f69674dd2> Ticker * Im Machtkampf bei N26 sind zumindest mal die umstrittenen Aufsichtsratspersonalien entschieden. The UK economic development bank, which invests in VC funds and startups, bagged an extra £6.6bn as part of the government's new industrial strategy, announced over the summer. A lot of that money will be invested across eight sectors the government defined as “growth-driving” in its summer report, including advanced manufacturing, creative industries, life sciences and clean energy. A chunk will also go to defence, an area where the bank is looking to do more deals, a trend that has captured European tech in the last couple of years. Defence and dual-use startups raised €1.85bn last year across 71 deals; so far this year they've raised €3.7bn across 126 deals, according to Sifted Opendoor warrants Normal shareholders of normal companies want the stock to go up. Shareholders of meme stock companies want that, but they also want something else<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/xBVVdkcivjqyttcGyVav2I8KLiUFXTOBDbAXwlMVPY7ki9HNRBc2isXRH7r4pr-zPM71Jj9RW_wj9ZWBHnq47jC9XulGamxnFZqAzOucsiVLprYOVmzvkzIr1dDH0o00Jvgp7vp4rd9vg4Bc4QOsY6_DsxJakcS2RB1re56IR_3ynZ3O4Xyxmm5KylsBn_7IN-u6YLd9IUaCfK-2LuQ0EEDJXcnQ4OTYRjRb9mAEfdkdk4cx6lauLmuosc4inmX2lsCqUIK0lNhwsyeWHjvzyjZETOSFCVAyKTfHYu3n5Cwvvu5C2yTsmPw-NMSTcanJgm7ot2JUnjo1gTP6N3I5qtbEusbTWzsj6EacAh-mMCFYy8cYTpqSywqViA/UfjEOwUV3cq9M5ohreiPCE_IsBKnarCg/14>. The additional thing that they want can perhaps be labeled “fun,” and it comes in various forms. AMC Entertainment Holdings Inc. was a big and self-conscious meme stock, and it amused its shareholders by giving them popcorn<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/HWSNgMCtVosYfmKVIFHqdDIX0tjJp8uZk-iSLUUdySqIjq_hCAf9nBmSwqtFlzyMQvQgT2nk8iXjLhDwi6st4v-KHjbIwm93qjLyVUzkDT4GQdiT0-4D3BnpphbmRGQRR48ld6q1IZIUZAf1p6WtOznyFxsdH98-D17Rt78MGI12dZBFua61xnGkchDe_HVVRVohMKhvev5bzYyjbzVlTvX2D_97C8cV4lman_-eMeJ5ktcu5jxEIpkkOYc0MQwh0zvkLhFqqwG-hDKzTaoGqXIzlNKgkhZdtwcxHKHyqR434UgZURjfHKpzmlTxScbGpr9_EyGyFrp2sjuUQ6Et8QtfI627vuWyk7LzF7LQXenAT04f1N-gisQBNQ/_ohg2g_hZeQyP4gVRhAp69zqMxwqC-PJ/14> and buying a gold mine<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/Yjncxf9wa0HrRltcN55k-DtoZUi-3oIoUCGdiWtawhKmLuvAuWxpuTlLQyl8IFPX-dgGQCQ8sWi8oKg5lr9gVZHjH7_9Pro_2tuEBzuLvT9UigDbUtPKZVhL_oU1qcYXfVwEL3y9v7MyDRN0N1KykzTLsPAvlgpRRirPfx3IuJLycV9Lb1UzcUoCOjfyQOjVYxWjR_PE_41nqpYOV8xs6GFtNO9wD9zVPk6RVz_-E1M_--2yi-gAy-5H9WlQnbToQCMMpykZQwET-SHMA1IzERRj7Wwn0iPHMvNmv9LO75k6cTi34VAe17TWgezZ9Zn7dazmm63-NNpIjKOxttcv3fZMUzpVGqpaYKGwo9wrzbylwGniN-O7LkoLlw/S1FrJXb5Chl6Ft8tsJGzdm1fH4KNw5cD/14> and having its chief executive officer do a YouTube interview with no pants on<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/qgNWjgZuzKnKIwkcyRVw8zOFA6gFe4GLDBy3oU7BOqTBgk0cGQE1ETh-WwMPUbc_epG7-X7y2UDrd-snlT_yu84nMLGLaS9Da-JnK0pc1tJkAxiZ7XkUxHxN574Z7W6fqNxE8hFvzjgzuqNl0oJ3LmrhKx8ZGiEy1inH_uKsIFj3SZZIzIYjAZqxBhVoIs3Vrs5t5zOwOV8Itv0ZXPT_xhbD1-ubi3PQixdgJ9Tyw1b7rqdYoo1qT3tL_sWpa9xCe31tLutO-8A5vEjoMNQq6M79OgyPWtkkrHuOmRajNTaQZOQqgALyIg5CACzOFQmqBAGmKoXiidhMhHXqyEgqq9OK-0Uvb5NFfq1Kv0EtRTuS_FtNQm_ODd2KjQ/tvo20JYFIW2MzYmzW159XCiJ2rJPiVBc/14>. Those techniques are not in the corporate finance textbooks, but they made sense in AMC's situation. If AMC's “Apes” (as its retail shareholders called themselves) were engaged and entertained, they would buy the stock, and the stock would go up, and AMC would be able to clear out its debts<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/R52ERisP3YoSl0xo0vP2R4qWiETlrXXTWEsybRmbYThrKshlKLHPoiZiHtawTR0CDsbK3i8AJ-SmHDd3vwmX10IOmq-OqvLB7rGxlXG0_dvW-6nVaEzPt8FkFDFjeHwwzKQb8JKwrSdXsaLh1VUFaIQ20dZhv3qyw-28GCbZ6OXoxWOPK5tnzhlYqoLdfWON4wesx4DsYwUJ3szdIQHmCUJrZNl2QXGujYHFtW-7BPfVnPTKsbXnLE5YfQogAneK76AHsfsLA6Ml13ZTXiRzHE-OqQtyhc2nxL4u-OXWZ8ahSkL6KjVvZwbMyjGIoXf6JV7X0Zl6RbKL5gBc4yuW2i6GkByWuB-bpIrJqIMuqyNYo0tyzWcfWPmugA/f_kvcBQv3F8eGoINFzYYHTzZmVF3lrX0/14> and stabilize its financial position. So, no pants. Is there some more general approach? Popcorn will not make sense for every company, and not every CEO is naturally entertaining on social media. But that's okay. Most of what makes a meme stock fun is: 1. A social media community, not run by the company, that enjoys talking about the stock, and 2. [Moon emoji<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/I4mawm-evYS-Hv_M5xAT7D6EduoAZhgceGnzDxdP6lxl8RgSKp3n3vndRcXnkot5HS5WD8n40kiFsOFnTUXrh_57KE2VvicflL4YC4duK-phFpnDgylJvWdAelR-PXrFL0ivqtUOhZoTTvDO3mDA6N9eOM5mV5Am1DYIimhIHPvXhePke9wWuoEETxKGaQQsnDfXmY8xgI_z9YNndvnUntY9Jho1hva9UfkoZnDM_dPUWsBJccrronIhiTELslwD_ELqOdk4gtWlXJncNPegc4-EJ6zAIujomaCaUxihwcbKEbW2Z8MVdGL98MuVMMtLgd3FvrsTY7MuePIeZ0Z__gMGZhNb-UxxphXapxulMHvnRCpk3H1rem34J6s/F9Ts8RhPE3D28HmYmxzWBCp4DA5bhhrn/14>]: What is specifically fun in a meme stock is its volatility, the possibility of going to the moon, the dream that if you buy the stock at $5 it might go to $500 tomorrow. So options trading goes great with meme stocks: Buying call options amplifies your gains if the stock goes up; you can invest a little bit in call options now and get back a lot if the stock goes up as you hope (and lose your investment if it doesn't). You can transform a somewhat lottery-ticket-like investment in a meme stock into a much more lottery-ticket-like investment in meme-stock options. That is an obvious and quite general form of fun. Opendoor knows<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/aw5wrNGLDzsahd-Zb4E1tEquG9yu2IepkJROnf9sflpwlNJ0rUxTak3DQlxQZ8aF5BspdsVhCHB_OmY_5iCOzb0Z5adcSkX1KWIjqRpN5xCE8WgxYf34vxBA43Zkuo1VkRweWr_T75WViA2GqVodwBD2z6Ne844gMBFtYSrM_2I2F30AH2IDFB-IgnzWrcj3PxigueIZpzIfaFMnTT29sXmI19gBBh1BUcjR1M8gsqYq8kBP9ru5SWMXXTkjD6b4f3vBg-5YQU-0EcUmtFJokdlavaQIHvJG34XY31RWIIQa5W52foADW4UsU6mRFMzi0AsUbfCGEYNBeRHPFHJA17Kd90GxA3wuXRCaS8RFu0oqRFJGl9_qErzmANI/6opbVtK-VAeB5Gst2-L9vbyXDyB2ewsd/14>: [Thursday], Opendoor Technologies Inc. (Nasdaq: OPEN) (“Opendoor” or the “Company”) announced a special dividend distribution of warrants to holders of the Company's common stock as of 5:00 p.m. New York City time on November 18, 2025 (the “Record Date”). The goal is simple: if management gets performance-based upside, shareholders should too - these warrants help achieve that. “To everyone who chose to be on this journey with us - thank you. You have been critical to this rebirth, and you should share in the upside just as we in management do,” said Opendoor CEO Kaz Nejatian. “Public markets have a long history of taking shareholders for granted - this program is built to reverse that.” This program is intentionally structured as a new playbook for public-company alignment. If the stock gets above $9, you can exercise your Series K warrant and buy a share for $9, and again with the other series at $13 and $17. Opendoor has given its shareholders some stock options. Let me go through some of the things that are going on here. First, Opendoor explains that this is analogous to executive stock options: “If management gets performance-based upside, shareholders should too.” The normal theory of executive stock options is that shareholders are diversified but managers are not: The typical shareholder of a typical public company wants the company to take positive-expected-value risks (because she benefits from the upside and has diversified away much of the risk), but the typical manager of that company has most of her net worth and career tied up in that company and might not want to take much risk. Stock options give the manager the proper incentives: If she takes risks and succeeds, her options pay out; if she takes no risks, she gets no rewards. That is, giving managers options aligns them with shareholders who hold stock. But giving the shareholders options makes them even more risk-loving. These warrants will be more valuable (1) if the stock goes up, sure (but the stock will also be more valuable if the stock goes up - if the stock gets to $17, the shareholders will be thrilled with or without warrants) but also (2) if the stock's volatility is high. The point of giving managers options is to align them with shareholders; the point of giving shareholders options is to ... align them with managers? Make them like volatility a bit more? Make them meme-ier? Second, one advantage of these warrants is that they automatically bring in money if the stock price goes up: If the stock trades above the warrant strike prices for a while, holders will exercise the warrants and pay Opendoor cash for more shares. Clase, meanwhile, was making millions of dollars a year from his baseball salary.) “Through this scheme, the defendants defrauded betting platforms, deprived Major League Baseball and the Cleveland Guardians of their honest services, illegally enriched themselves and their co-conspirators, misled the public, and betrayed America's pastime.” I think there are two main theories of what makes this illegal. The first theory is that they “defrauded betting platforms.” Online sportsbooks offer prop bets on things like whether “a specific pitch would be either a ball or a batter hit by pitch, as opposed to a strike” or “the speed of a given pitch, such as whether the pitch would be above 94.95 miles per hour.” [5] When the sportsbooks offer these bets, they expect that the bettors do not have inside information, and the sportsbooks' terms of service specifically prohibited users from betting if they “had access to any pre-release, confidential information or other information that was not available to all other wagerers, including any information provided by a professional athlete.” The people who allegedly bet on Ortiz's and Clase's pitches thus violated the sportsbooks' terms of service. This, in the Justice Department's theory, is fraud. We talked about this theory<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/-QoBYYAbkIYeJizYS3LFeWy8N4UxsH9OZBLEtLAFCc1j6rwsi0IvPfKPvIvvJzwABnIaiixsq7kDjn9HusvdFTShf7uwEnbmU3HucIhRntvU0JjvYidi6QJiAOU7-PEjDpeWKeL-ZZiGbdLWtrfqrgbsGoVRWuNsfvsNWGbJ-LTEAIajWiouaOP1EAVGLebxpmeskE139Q-uiTd5yGJF_tHlhoL7qYXdhkSQbtpsJTY8FAUjaLwmmGd_xShimHbO_Y38ZSdVn4c8vSynAD6FGn9b1MiMMTc18pQ8anUmZOVGe6LYq2Lo9aZjRhuA8v-kOqeaig5WLuaQauwjNSDEogPnUYZ4Wu8pLy6rt9yX6Zfilocydz1RsXwnXq0/7QKeaRi0D63kgXAlK2zKN3VnhQrsct_Y/14> a couple of weeks ago, when some bettors were charged with betting using inside information about basketball players. It is, I wrote, a somewhat weird theory, essentially giving the sportsbooks' terms of service - which nobody reads! - the force of criminal law. Still there is something intuitively correct about it; it does feel like insider betting is a scam on the person you're betting against. The theory is slightly weirder here, though, as Ortiz and Clase are not charged with betting. They had no reason to read the sportsbooks' terms of service, since they were not customers of the sportsbooks. So they are not actually charged with fraud on the sportsbooks; they are charged with conspiracy. Their gambler buddies allegedly defrauded the sportsbooks by violating their terms of service; Ortiz and Clase are charged with conspiring to violate the terms of service. Kind of a strange crime. The other theory is that they “deprived Major League Baseball and the Cleveland Guardians of their honest services.” “Honest services wire fraud” is the somewhat odd legal term of art for “taking bribes”: The theory is that if you take a bribe to do something against the interests of your employer, you are committing fraud on the employer by depriving them of your “honest services.” The classic US Supreme Court case<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/6ScHxn1g-125nFrjt-3tinYLVVZ9xTvGjfAf0qkUnPrb5h8cZHvn6R-2JZhqWzDkKBFkPYpPXj9-4HYPD7ptq_WMd9VsrDSv19rWB0lZGoe5kggjUJvV_egRUJphsAxuAoiP7ykeUHsvR7dqx97O13VCaPn0_agY5nfiPf3EXyJcSQnY25RKJQffJ8kwOQ8iFOWoDLi8nMnTl1_1iW3vEZp-OJpwa_5Iaeh-Cg1H2YG-3FYtTcO6csYrgsvNW7kp0KupF4pY64XQ6sw6rSV3fmW3eO6_ZD1CAYQq-rPWTQuG4cy7dyIk6nmolGfF6C9xX-S-e2uZT2FGUTxzR_2hrMY5yKaOv8xQF56SIzu6gMKf2mswmxPusZdvci8/1f1rT-FAuvtcY8ItfWboNNh3npv56SeB/14> involved Jeff Skilling, and held that honest services fraud involves “fraudulent schemes to deprive another of honest services through bribes or kickbacks supplied by a third party who had not been deceived.” Fine, fair enough: Here, Ortiz and Clase are charged with not doing their best for the Guardians and the game of baseball (by throwing some balls in the dirt), because they got paid by their gambler friends. It's possible that this intervention was a bit Trumpy, but I think there is a decent argument that the Novo structure was designed to get around the normal US antitrust pre-approval rules, and in a way that might be bad for competition. That is, ordinarily, two companies sign a merger and then take it to the FTC for approval before the deal closes. If the FTC says no, the deal doesn't close, and there's no big competitive harm. Here, though, Novo would pay Metsera before getting FTC approval, and would then spend up to two years trying to get that approval. Meanwhile Metsera's drugs would be off the market, whereas if Pfizer bought Metsera it would presumably try to commercialize those drugs as quickly as possible. Pfizer's theory was that Novo's structure was intended, not to buy Metsera, but just to block Pfizer from buying it. title: FW: 11/11/25: Mambu wächst nur noch schwach, Kunden versus Trade Republic
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Tuesday, 11 November 2025 06:15:07 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 11/11/25: Mambu wächst nur noch schwach, Kunden versus Trade Republic Außerdem: Acht Fragen zur Deutschen Bank, Wieso die Coba-Aktie steilgeht [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/e40e4f4a-9191-ea2c-acd1-889d7bf8f5ab.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=e2ddabb34c&e=8f69674dd2> Von Sewing bis M&A  um diese acht Fragen geht's jetzt bei der Deutschen Bank Welchen Verlauf hätte die Bankengeschichte eigentlich genommen, wenn die Unicredit sich vor einem Jahr nicht die Commerzbank als Zielobjekt ausgesucht hätte  sondern gleich die Deutsche Bank? Wäre Andrea Orcel dann am Sonntag, den 22. September 2024, völlig unvermittelt auf der Terrasse von Christian Sewing aufgekreuzt ("Buongiorno, Cristiano")? Hätte die Deutsche Bank mit einer "Proud2BeBlue"-Kampagne einen seltsamen Marketing-Preis nach dem nächsten abgeräumt? Und vor allem: Wo stünde die Aktie des größten deutschen Kreditinstituts heute? Bei 40 Euro? Bei 50 Euro? Denn das eigentlich Unglaubliche ist ja: Seit dem Morgen des 11. September 2024, an dem der Einstieg der Unicredit bei der Commerzbank bekannt wurde, ist die Aktie der Deutschen Bank um rund 120% gestiegen. Ganz ohne Orcel auf der Terrasse. Ganz ohne Übernahmefantasien. Eigentlich ein Husarenstück! Mit der Folge, dass das, was bis vor einem Jahr als durchaus denkbar galt, nämlich dass die Deutsche Bank irgendwann mal zum Übernahmekandidaten werden könnte, für den Moment fast ausgeschlossen erscheint  angesichts einer Marktkapitalisierung von inzwischen wieder mehr als 60 Mrd. Euro. Oder anders gesagt: Das größte Geldhaus der Republik ist heute in einer Position (siehe auch jüngst unsere Analyse der Q3-Zahlen<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=6002c26a92&e=8f69674dd2>), die so kommod ist wie seit mindestens einer Dekade nicht mehr. Womit sich im Hinblick auf das große Strategie-Update am 17. November allerdings die Frage stellt, was denn jetzt noch kommen soll. Zumal ein paar Punkte ja offen sind: Wie will das Institut mit der inzwischen fast unheimlichen Machtfülle von Vorstandschef Sewing umgehen? Wer wird nach dem Abgang von Finanzchef James von Moltke die neue Nummer 2? Oder auch, ganz verwegen: Wenn die Deutsche Bank kein Übernahmekandidat mehr ist  wird sie dann selbst zum Akquisiteur? Eine Bestandsaufnahme in acht Kapiteln. Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=72cb71bec3&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/1f355e5c-a37c-48c8-869a-69500bd0b72c.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=8d72c92b67&e=8f69674dd2> AI Regulierung  sind Sie bereit? Der EU AI Act zwingt Banken zum Handeln. Wer AI gewinnbringend nutzen will, braucht Regeln, Transparenz und technische Souveränität. Das Whitepaper zeigt, wie es geht  Best Practices inklusive. Jetzt Zugriff sichern.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=4f320caf88&e=8f69674dd2> Warum immer mehr Banken das Geschäft mit Schließfächern aufgeben (frei zugänglich) Sie gingen nicht durch die Decke  sondern kamen durch selbige. Mit einem Kernbohrer drangen Unbekannte im August 2021 aus einer darüber liegenden Wohnung in den Tresorraum einer Filiale der Hamburger Sparkasse ein. Dort brachen sie mehr als 600 Schließfächer auf und erbeuteten dabei Geld und Schmuck im Wert von  ja, von wie viel eigentlich? Rund 11 Mio. Euro, sagt die Haspa. Von rund 40 Mio. Euro war indes aufseiten der geschädigten Kunden die Rede. Jedenfalls war vier Jahre nach dem "Millionen-Coup von Norderstedt" der juristische Streit um die damaligen Ereignisse auch diesen Sommer noch in vollem Gange. Bis zu 40.000 Euro pro geschädigtem Kunden hatte die größte Sparkasse der Republik gezahlt. Zu wenig, sagten die Kunden-Anwälte. Die Sache wanderte zum Hamburger Oberlandesgericht, und die Kernfrage lautete: Hatte die Haspa den Tresorraum zum Zeitpunkt der Tat ausreichend abgesichert? Nein, sagte ein vom Hamburger Oberlandesgericht beauftragter Gutachter. In dessen Bericht hieß es: "Die Sicherheitsmaßnahmen [ ] haben nicht dem anerkannten Stand der Technik bzw. etablierten Branchenstandards für Bankfilialen vergleichbarer Größe und mit vergleichbaren Tresor- und Schließfachanlagen entsprochen." Bei dem Prozess ging es im Grunde aber um eine viel weitreichendere Frage: Lohnt sich für Banken und Sparkassen das Geschäft mit Schließfächern überhaupt noch? Oder müsste es nicht abgeschafft oder wenigstens ganz anders bepreist werden? Unser Deep Dive aus dem Juli  jetzt vor der Paywall: Finanz-Szene (7 Tage frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=d80ae6120a&e=8f69674dd2> News * Die Deutsche Bank steht laut Bloomberg (Paywall)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=64de5e028c&e=8f69674dd2> kurz vor dem Abschluss einer SRT-Verbriefung im Umfang von rund 1 Mrd. Euro  dabei soll es sich um ein Portfolio italienischer Autokredite handeln. Übernehmen wolle die Risiken die Europäische Investitionsbank (bzw. deren Fondsvehikel EIF). * Bei Trade Republic wächst die Zahl der Kundenbeschwerden schneller als die Zahl der Kunden. Von Januar bis September seien bei den 16 Verbraucherzentralen gut 300 Beschwerden eingegangen (also etwas mehr als eine pro Tag), vermeldet das Handelsblatt (Paywall)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=46e87a45de&e=8f69674dd2>  verglichen mit dem Vorjahreszeitraum ein Plus von 133%. It's widely considered inevitable that some in the country will see their taxes rise, as finance minister Rachel Reeves looks to balance the books of an increasingly creaking economy. Entrepreneurs could be in the firing line. Earlier this month, it was reported that Reeves was mulling an exit tax for those with shares in British assets. The sector has come out fighting. Yesterday lobby group Startup Coalition published a letter<https://email.sifted.eu/e3t/Ctc/LZ+113/d2mfCN04/VW0Lg44yBt_HW2pGF_z1p4SvWVJvnzy5FLk7pN1c6srH3qgz0W95jsWP6lZ3ljW2n2lvY3nvP8dW7bLrmT4H5YqLW7tkpLM5gvmsXVHpxyG21fyFDW8PfB4K46JnHvVwMdCm2xF8NJV-SwxZ6zcl3KW3LPBfW1Qgvs2W6g7n6-4mPDMdW1TwZ6-8bwTrlW7NC3Lv3RPD6KW1cbZNl8XGBz3W73b5tQ6G7tnNVGsfMb8LPkTcW9bQfxV5QcD9ZW5dRwNw3W1PYzW8N7DSV5fM50ZW4Qzp9g8PTQT-W6dWFsH3btCMyW7lybD94YpxB9N7w_lG4gpT18W97QM8t476zGqW3MPlPB25ZCGyW5p2Rmx25w3kFW8dJPsv5CTlJdW6SqJ5Q2F2Mn8W2m11Tq7hB8ZfW5D4VDG216JKzW164Kj84KyVjKMhnx4F4WfXxf7vkTh604> signed by 150+ entrepreneurs and investors urging Reeves to reconsider. Signatories include energy startup Fuse founder Alan Chang, 20VC's Harry Stebbings, Project Europe chief Kitty Mayo, AI fintech Cleo founder Barney Hussey-Yeo and Wise and Plural founder Taavet Hinrikus. VCs from Dawn Capital, Episode 1 and Notion Capital also signed. The letter warns that “a potential exit tax would not only tell founders that their ideas and innovations aren't welcome, but that they should either get out early or not come at all.” Time will tell if HM Treasury heeds the warning. November 2025 Der Tag Das Wichtigste aus der Wirtschaft ­ [https://cdn.prod.www.manager-magazin.de/images/8a678134-820c-433a-bb0b-97273c4c1e33_w112_r1_fpx55.01_fpy51.34.jpg] Hannah Steinharter Redakteurin manager magazin Lieber Herr Frignani. In den Karnevalshochburgen des Landes hieß es heute Punkt 11.11 Uhr: Helau und Alaaf! Kostümierte Jecken haben die fünfte Jahreszeit ausgelassen begrüßt  mit Konfetti, Krapfen und bei bester Laune. Ob Sie nun mitten im Getümmel standen oder den Tag lieber ignoriert haben: An der Börse könnte bald ebenfalls ein vertrautes Saisonphänomen starten  die Jahresendrallye. Studien zeigen, dass Kurse zum Jahresende häufig stärker anziehen als in anderen Monaten. Und einiges spricht dafür, dass das in diesem Jahr auch so sein wird. Mein Kollege Christoph Rottwilm hat sich angesehen, welche Werte dabei in diesem Jahr die Favoriten wären. Den Überblick gibt es hier: Was Anleger über die Jahresendrallye 2025 wissen sollten (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294ff45b766c52e20da121b09c7306e29b7ce48ab4df2c8f8466d15a50c7f889b47192ae5d35050c07c2766a56a6de0991a063a8aa3c14db95b8>. ANZEIGE [desktop] <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294fcb86d0d7defb2c21420b3e4e5af45706f31731b9fb6d2ca157b97ebe74acaa90f1ea4aa992cb2f486102e8007505b26ef6d74bd122dfc510> [mobile] <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294fcb86d0d7defb2c21420b3e4e5af45706f31731b9fb6d2ca157b97ebe74acaa90f1ea4aa992cb2f486102e8007505b26ef6d74bd122dfc510> [Vorn dabei: Die Aktien von Rheinmetall, Palantir und Robinhood dominierten 2025 bislang die Indizes Dax, Nasdaq 100 und S&P 500] Vorn dabei: Die Aktien von Rheinmetall, Palantir und Robinhood dominierten 2025 bislang die Indizes Dax, Nasdaq 100 und S&P 500 [M] Uwe Koch / HMB-Media / IMAGO, Fabrice Coffrini / AFP, Mark Lennihan / AP [separator] Die Wirtschaftsnews des Tages: * Softbank-Gründer Masayoshi Son (68) nimmt ordentlich Gewinne mit: Der japanische Techinvestor hat seinen kompletten Bestand an Nvidia-Aktien versilbert und dabei rund 5,8 Milliarden US-Dollar<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f696f2e854314304c001381661487ec7d51cf82a9e43f82b42580991eb78641dc69b90bbda42ff7db9de3f47bed516466870264cedb6f5359> erlöst. Auf den KI-Boom setzt Softbank aber weiterhin. * US-Starinvestor Warren Buffett (95) hat sich in seinem wohl letzten Brief als Chef der Holding Berkshire Hathaway an die Aktionäre gewandt. Darin stellt er sich  kurz vor seinem Rücktritt zum Jahresende  deutlich hinter seinen Nachfolger Greg Abel (63)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f4dc97ba87e9723751c4def1b22fdf04c6486e9ae8f0969556c2bf11a12004e28e4bb4370fd3f8e1c7e834c7f51855c43793a0a3ae007ce22>. * Die deutsche Industrie schlägt derweil Alarm. Laut einer Ifo-Umfrage sieht sie die eigene Wettbewerbsfähigkeit auf einem neuen Tiefpunkt. Besonders dramatisch ist die Situation in den energieintensiven Unternehmen<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f25002bb3d209def291a77ffecf777028e397a32570b677e5ce71776cf5ae5a776c04815f77d4ce442c2a832119a1bea96c4b861e41700ac3>. * Zu guter Letzt konnte die deutsche Verwertungsgesellschaft Gema einen Etappensieg vor Gericht für sich verbuchen  und das ausgerechnet gegen den ChatGPT-Anbieter OpenAI. Im Streit um die Nutzung der Texte von Songs wie Über den Wolken oder In der Weihnachtsbäckerei erging ein Urteil, das noch größere Auswirkungen haben könnte<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294fe335b6dfcff4d9bd9107e0d7d7c61ea30c9858ec597d2226dadf83c308e5c81639810e6ed1007a00611c7ecb19e10254507fe3bb5ac3dabe>. [separator] Die Personalien des Tages: [Abgang: KI-Experte Yann LeCun verlässt Meta] Abgang: KI-Experte Yann LeCun verlässt Meta Bloomberg / Getty Images * KI-Spezialisten können sich ihre Jobs momentan beinahe aussuchen, die Fluktuation ist daher hoch. Jüngstes Beispiel: Bei Meta hat mit Yann LeCun (65) einer der wichtigsten KI-Forscher seinen Abgang angekündigt<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f76c82e81b491dcc48fe0bbbd4c05e595c2521a4a5aefc2085c99602f8db010cb1fc10261e632a4b5b4be1e2b2786e530739bf19f04bbe770>. Auch Intel muss eine KI-Spitzenkraft an die Konkurrenz ziehen lassen. [separator] Was uns sonst noch beschäftigt hat: * Elke und Andreas Hartleif (beide 59) produzieren mit ihrer Firma Veka Kunststoffprofile für Fenster und Türen. Die Plastikleisten sehen auf den ersten Blick nicht besonders spannend aus, haben das Unternehmen aus dem Münsterland aber zum Weltmarktführer gemacht. Warum Fensterbauer aus der ganzen Welt auf die Leisten von Veka zählen und wie es den Hartleifs gelingt, der Billigkonkurrenz zu trotzen, lesen Sie hier: Eine Firma mit klarem Profil (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f77c5647a96a714d35f59ff4c0ca993ab3d9a5f34e204e8c5ea7c15725c50cfacbc0f543a537e18379db3f73ee536551d1e755471cb7bdf13>. * Die Preise für Luxusgüter wie Oldtimer, Schmuck oder Kunstobjekte haben lange Zeit immer neue Rekorde aufgestellt. Diese Preisrallye ist zwar vorerst beendet, das Investment kann sich aber weiterhin lohnen. Zum Verständnis helfen: Drei Grafiken, die Luxusinvestoren kennen sollten (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294fb5884be3cfb3915a078819d2d4493d26ec3922b9034428da62554b08283310b45a352ac8cb8831b1a394a9f5ccc462f98604fcd273004846>. [separator] Was Ihnen in Ihrem Unternehmen helfen könnte: * Das österreichische Familienunternehmen Giesswein hat auf sich ein Experiment eingelassen: Ein Jahr lang hat der Schuhhersteller ChatGPT in Vorstandssitzungen genutzt. Also: Was passiert eigentlich, wenn die KI in der Geschäftsführung sitzt? Die Antwort gibt es beim Harvard Business manager (HBm+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f8a3b45c532f99558c22b1b8937fcebc3e2962586eb4f7a49a630e0f75a32ba6abdff423815086a52210638dfee3634cd5b818b22e886ad79>. * Die Kollegen unserer Weiterbildungsplattform manage  forward beschäftigen sich in einer neuen Masterclass ebenfalls mit künstlicher Intelligenz. KI-Experte und Agenturchef Timm Rotter erklärt, wie KI den gesamten Marketingprozess optimieren kann  von der Zielgruppenanalyse über die Entwicklung von Kampagnenideen bis zur Erstellung konkreter Anzeigen und Texte. Und das Beste: Mit dem Code RICHTIGGUTERRABATTCODE erhalten Sie 20 Prozent Rabatt auf den Eintrittspreis. Zur Anmeldung einmal hier entlang bitte<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f388f529a3f6f0c7efe019bd0d67dd3c72db04c03928d9339d5f067665af89b82e9c5e0b19370051d1ec37c32c077d13fab740c183861c3b2>. [separator] Meine Empfehlung für den Abend: [Einsteigerin: Gründerin Annemarie Heyl fand mit dem Safthersteller Kale & Me eine neue Erfüllung] Einsteigerin: Gründerin Annemarie Heyl fand mit dem Safthersteller Kale & Me eine neue Erfüllung Aliona Kardash / manager magazin * Die Nachfolge im familieneigenen Unternehmen zu organisieren, sorgt vielerorts regelmäßig für Krisen. Denn wo Menschen privat wie beruflich in engstem Kontakt miteinander stehen, gibt es viel Konfliktpotenzial. Meine Kollegin Julia Hackober hat mit mehreren Unternehmern und Gründerinnen gesprochen, bei denen der Weg nicht wie ursprünglich gedacht an die Spitze der Familienfirma führte, sondern anderswohin. Warum diese Menschen aus dem Geplanten ausgestiegen sind, wie sie diese Entscheidung fürs Leben geprägt hat  und wie es ihnen gelungen ist, die Familie daran nicht zerbrechen zu lassen, lesen Sie hier: Familienunternehmen  wenn Nachfolge keine Option ist (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=a565060b64a3294f37df2a58195da7862023935f9f0afd998b65a84d13f493a7aac691dbbc310364b7226cf5a3cc53f230c1f985158b3f7d68fe4a7ae5343934>.
