Hedge fund competition The basic thesis<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/8BHemS2u23-QveH4KLXcl-2FUwGV_nkqp6XcJtRtc-bwWHO6Z1Rnj1m_CmRsPTNxoRV0nd57GXP8aVjdrWTNXktjPe7YwEV7Ew9oorTQjxEWi0UQq_ZQF6bQRYlI0qeKvF73tu5rAhiLllTodKU9oMobz54tcqC74afgw2VlISva2XmCjGqwmhQsWSr0914UoHWxHik6tZAE-gtKIQb4dyB447gGzN4VQ9pyTWhowdKu3RgWpk8d-UHHnyW_7I60-m_rGavVIvraF81swk-4TIpzNRgXfVdyWOh2JrjOvZYXyXgMjL5zVvSO7JdpEcUgRjN1WrliLW3jHVGPek5ktPY_m_9YsUWShswKwa3f9qVUz1tACVdtsmMOiA/ETavYMZ7tgtFt_37IzLiJEsrVJX8PgND/14> of the big multistrategy multimanager pod shop hedge funds is that investing talent is real, identifiable and scarce. There are people who are reliably good at buying stocks that will go up and selling stocks that will go down; they have an investing process that works, so if you give them a billion dollars to manage they will earn steady market-beating returns. The big hedge fund firms are essentially in the business of finding those people; they have a investor hiring process that works  theyre a massive filter of talent<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/VpTDFg64cDs-f3eD5Z_1xYZ3C3FKWs5vAFHFHJzSRAvrCsbEMSUgl2MlVbCDof8b02KRdPzZ2QyOz6LiukTbEfGdyRkWmdzhHgpJBTsPK8G0bUj364Uo9otiu6kA2og75U5MlHIl4A6ndCb8AyZsDe0SDHjK1oxDbGUi4fjin2FqArA3IejjWMGUBzitgqcQ33-KQ46fRYBW_KX0Gl0MDKc1Ev0KbLxeK16XZvTqAheDnfU6LYP3WENtSNGYc4wYRbM851IgYjYwKdID2lhZzVVxeqYAFZINNRsfEbfCOII-ASxcDHtizhcMgH-2W-3kzfG8Hztg6EH22ySit-og9m_atV1jMMQq0WKhxRvtN_Gp5c-w-czbuF4wGA/yeU1jHwD6paujZlKoxKfU2-OK7gTaCxJ/14>  so they can run tens of billions of dollars of assets and allocate them to the best possible investors. But this talent is rare, so the people who have it can command a high price, generally 20% or more of the returns they generate, often with tens of millions of dollars guaranteed. And because it is so rare, the big funds have to constantly poach people from smaller funds, and from each other, to fill their seats and generate returns for investors. One amusing irony of this situation is that hedge fund manager talent is artificially scarce. Perhaps there are, say, 5,000 good portfolio managers in the world. How many of them are managing portfolios at any given time? On some plausible assumptions the answer might be 3,000. At Business Insider, Bradley Saacks reports<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/Durvvt9f63XXuOZc_TqVluNJG6BmboK0DwSLmK5FDrZbZjP8lrm4CCW9imgqVOgMjwYCeGhr1APuKZlH5_9_Le9wdjV_nEREPzNCGOu6LAig12v5iocr1XvbTl_WH9oAz27mA5Re4HPGoWNtfmAJ69KF3gVoPmX6DnJrjlNP02Ie42hLiAkVL5O-u27n48wCTJW469yv8dSgNnU-EA7N5THFKuzkHHlM4kR97Lc2ql1f_AZXUebui_cdIZeyUKpWusMx8kg2lYMiSWfN5WGNza2_TlUUZ0l8du7YTfSlqslGfOMapsMvNnpqPrvkrlGZ2412su_4Z5XoX0YBHA5NUgfezPxQtN7IzowyNrDHiXixiNHg7vFm32W0qA/qwOkDg6ShicJc0WwmVu4HlVysj1GMSq8/14> on the hedge fund talent competition: It's not uncommon for a portfolio manager to work for two or three of the top funds over a five-year span, including breaks to avoid violating non-compete clauses in their contracts. A PM who gets fired on a Tuesday often has an inbox full of suitors by Wednesday, and some PMs are even getting re-hired by firms that once pink-slipped them for losing money. Historically, capital was the bottleneck, says one investor in several big-name hedge funds, who asked to remain anonymous in order to speak candidly. Now it's 100% talent. If you work for three funds over five years, then those five years will include two gardening leaves, and if youre senior enough the gardening leaves could easily be a year or more. So you work for maybe three out of five years. Thats probably not everyones experience, but still. A meaningful chunk of the available portfolio managers are actually out of the market in any given year. In a world of scarce fixed supply, that has to push up prices. Saacks quotes Izzy Englander, who runs Millennium Management: At a 2023 event with fellow hedge-fund billionaire Paul Tudor Jones, Englander said that long non-compete agreements had helped create a talent bubble and an artificially small pool of potential hires that can demand more, according to a source who was in attendance for the talk. If you are a hedge fund portfolio manager, is this the optimal way to arrange your life? Like, I will be on vacation for two out of every five years, and when I do work I will get paid a huge premium for my services because there arent enough people like me to go around? I feel like when I put it like that it sounds pretty great? Still I bet a bunch of hedge-fund PMs would prefer less gardening leave. If you love allocating capital and correcting market inefficiencies, it is tough to be out of the game for years at a time. Anyway the story is mostly about how frantic the competition for talent is, and how the big hedge fund managers are annoyed that their hired guns, who they trained over decades to be mercenaries, are behaving like mercenaries. And: Millennium alone hired around 160 new portfolio managers last year  an average of three a week  according to a person close to the firm. That's equivalent to the entire workforce of $50 billion Tiger Global, according to regulatory filings. "Does the universe create that many people who you haven't already seen every year?" says an executive whose firm competes with the Big Four. Counterpoint: Yes? Obviously? The universe creates more than 100 million new people every year. Those new people are not immediately useful to hedge fund managers, fine, but colleges create millions of new graduates every year. Theyre not immediately useful either, but theyre closer: Much like private equity 15 years ago, multistrategy funds have reached a maturation point, and the shift has necessitated a more traditional workplace culture and structure. Citadel, Point72, and Balyasny have all built training programs for college students and fresh graduates in hopes of creating an internal talent pipeline that fuels a sense of connection to the fund that gave them their first job. Partnership stakes in the business and longer-term financial incentives are becoming more common. Balyasny, for example, added three new partners last year, all of whom are PMs. Point72's Academy program, launched a decade ago, has produced more than 200 analysts. I have sometimes mused about an alternative model of the big multistrategy hedge funds. First Brands One thing that some companies do is borrow against their accounts receivable: You sell some stuff to some customers, the customers have 60 days to pay you, you want money now, so you bundle together a bunch of invoices and sell them to a lender. You get money now, and when the customers pay you in 60 days, you give the money to the lender. Probably when you first do this, the lender will come in and do some due diligence and talk to the customers and make sure this is all a good credit risk. But after youve been doing it for a while, everyone will get increasingly comfortable, and you can just email over 1,000 PDF invoices to the lender and get back cash the same day. This creates an obvious problem, which is that you have to pay back the extra money, and there is no actual extra customer money coming in. So probably in 60 days you will have to do this again, but more so: Youll have to make even more fake invoices to borrow even more money to pay back the money you borrowed from the previous fake invoices. And this snowballs. Probably when you first do this, it is a wrenching moral quandary that you keep quiet out of shame and fear. Zuckerberg has pivoted away from the longer-term research work of Metas Fundamental AI Research Lab (Fair), which LeCun has headed since 2013, to focus on more rapidly rolling out models and AI products after deciding that Meta had fallen behind the competition. Zuckerbergs pivot followed the botched release of Metas most recent Llama 4 model, which performed worse than the most advanced offerings from Google, OpenAI and Anthropic, while its Meta AI chatbot has failed to gain traction with consumers. LeCun, however, has long argued that the LLMs that Zuckerberg has put at the centre of his strategy are useful but will never be able to reason and plan like humans, increasingly appearing at odds with his bosss AI vision. Within Fair, LeCun has instead focused on developing an entirely new generation of AI systems that he hopes will power machines with human-level intelligence, known as world models. These systems aim to understand the physical world by learning from videos and spatial data rather than just language, though LeCun has said it could take a decade to fully develop the architecture. From this telling of the story, it does sound like Meta and Zuckerberg are prioritizing short-term rollouts and monetization of current AI models over long-term fundamental research. Zuckerberg has come under growing pressure from Wall Street to show that his multibillion-dollar investment in becoming an AI leader will pay off and boost revenue, reports the FT, and tinkering with world models for a decade is not the way to boost revenue today. I wrote: If you are a top AI researcher, probably a lot of your friends are also top AI researchers. If you all got together, you could (1) hang out and have fun and (2) also do some top AI research. And then you could go out to investors and say hey, look, top AI researchers here, give us a billion dollars. And if the investors said yes but what are you all doing together, you could give them a disapproving look and take a step toward the door, and they would say were so sorry, we dont know what we were thinking, to make it up to you heres $2 billion. And then youd have $2 billion dollars to hang out with your friends. And do top AI research with them, if you want. You probably do want! Thats how you got to be top AI researchers. But do you need to do boring stuff like have a business plan or pursue revenue? I dont I dont really see why you would? It is really an amazing time to be an AI researcher. You can come into work to pursue pure science, uncontaminated by any need for near-term practical applications or making money. And when your boss comes to you and says hey guy not to be annoying but I am paying you $100 million, is there any way we could turn any of this stuff into money, you can quit in a huff and find venture capitalists who will give you billions of dollars to be even less commercial. And theyre not even wrong! Betting on long-term theoretical AI research has turned out to be hugely lucrative for a lot of investors; theres no reason not to keep doing it. Its a golden age of academic researchers getting bazillions of dollars to pursue pure research. OpenAI expects thinner margins than Anthropic from its sales for the next five years. Yet it is investing far more in the chips and data centers needed to build its AI technology, and doling out more stock-based compensation to attract top researchers. I guess lose lots of money now to become the dominant player is traditional long-term thinking, while live within our means and grow gradually is more of the public-company approach. But in AI the stakes are different, and rush to build a superintelligence as fast as we can is arguably a bit short-sighted. Tether gold traders If you gave me $100 for safekeeping, and I promised to give you back the $100 without interest in a year, and in the meantime I parked your $100 in a savings account at a big US bank, youd be like yeah sure sounds right. Thats the normal place to park dollars for safekeeping. If I parked your $100 in a money market mutual fund, or in US Treasury bills, that would be good and normal too. Microsoft Corp. bonds? Ehh maybe, sure, I guess, though there is more risk there. If I parked your $100 in Tesla Inc. stock, that would be significantly weirder. Tesla is volatile; it can go down; there is some probability that, in a year, I wont have $100 to give back to you. Maybe its fine: Broadly speaking Tesla mostly goes up, and theres a good chance that by putting your money in Tesla Ill have way more than enough to pay you back. But it seems like an unnecessary risk, and youd think it was kind of odd for me to do that. What if I parked your $100 in Bitcoin? Well, mostly, same answer: Bitcoin is volatile, it can go down, etc. If I parked your $100 in Bitcoin, you might reasonably say why did you do that? But I might have an answer. My answer  if I was the sort of person who took your $100 and parked it in Bitcoin  might have a certain hard-money flavor to it. My answer might be look, the dollar itself is not very stable; inflation and government debt are constantly eating away at its value, and the only way to preserve stable value is to put your money in hard assets like Bitcoin. [1] You might reasonably reply: What, no, that doesnt matter; you promised to give me back a specific number of dollars; if the dollar is debased or whatever that doesnt matter to our arrangement; all you have to do is give me the dollars back. If Bitcoin goes up against the dollar that wont help me; if Bitcoin goes down against the dollar then you wont have enough dollars for me. Youre just making a proprietary bet with my money. The stuff about debasement and preserving value is irrelevant; keep my dollars in dollars. This objection strikes me as obviously correct, but I think that some people will disagree. What if I parked your $100 in gold? My instinct is that the analysis is exactly the same as for Bitcoin: Gold can go down against the dollar, that would be bad, but I might go around saying like ooh debasement inflation ooh, got to get some hard assets in here to back your dollar claims. And you might reasonably find that incoherent: Your claim is for dollars, not for gold, and inflation is irrelevant to my obligations to you. Tether has aggressively expanded its presence in precious metals in recent years, amassing one of the worlds biggest hoards of gold outside of banks and nation states as part of its more than $180 billion in reserve assets. HSBC is a powerhouse in precious metals, widely seen as the largest player after JPMorgan Chase & Co., with operations spanning futures trading, vaulting and sending gold bars across the globe. Tether  which owns bullion as part of the reserves backing its flagship US dollar stablecoin  held more than $12 billion of the precious metal in September, according to its last reserves report. The El Salvador-based company has added to those holdings at an average rate of more than one ton a week in the year through September, according to Bloomberg calculations. That makes Tether one of the biggest buyers in the market, without including the bullion held against its own gold-backed stablecoin, or any private investments bought with Tethers billions of dollars of profits. The company has also taken stakes in other parts of the gold supply chain, including royalty companies. The Tether stablecoin, or USDT, is convertible on a one-to-one basis with the dollar, and relies on reserves mostly composed of US government debt, as well as other assets like gold. The company also issues the stablecoin Tether Gold, or XAUT, of which roughly $2 billion worth are in circulation, 100% backed by about 1,300 gold bars, according to a Tether website. title: FW: 12/11/25: Diese Sparkasse ist irre reich, Dieser Sparda geht‘s richtig mies
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene - Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Wednesday, 12 November 2025 06:14:22 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 12/11/25: Diese Sparkasse ist irre reich, Dieser Sparda geht‘s richtig mies Außerdem: J.P. Morgan schafft hunderte Berlin-Jobs, Dt. Bank setzt auf dt. Tandem [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/69fd6614-b124-afd1-a646-f535755d8bf5.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=7928674239&e=8f69674dd2> Exklusiv: Wie eine einfache Sparkasse >250 Mio. Euro mit einem Goldschatz verdiente Wie läuft das eigentlich ab, wenn so eine Primärbank plötzlich anfängt, seltsame Dinge zu tun? Wenn also, nur mal als Beispiel, die VR Bank Niederbayern-Oberpfalz in den Olivenanbau einsteigt. Oder die Altmüller-Volksbank ein Skigebiet erwirbt. Wir jedenfalls stellen uns das so vor, dass irgendwer Drittes (sei es ein Aufsichtsrat, ein Mitarbeiter, ein Strategieberater oder eine rasputineske Gestalt aus dem erweiterten Umfeld der Bank) dem Vorstandschef einen entsprechenden Floh ins Ohr setzt. Dann schläft der Vorstandschef eine Nacht drüber (wenn überhaupt). Und schließlich ruft er: Das ist aber eine tolle Idee! Womit die Sache durch die Gremien de facto schon halb durch ist. Und es also alsbald an die Umsetzung gehen kann. Jedenfalls: Exakt so oder womöglich ganz anders wird's vor ein paar Jahren auch bei jener mittelgroßen Sparkasse aus dem Südwesten der Republik gewesen sein, der wir uns heute Morgen ehrfurchtsvoll widmen wollen. Gold? Tonnenweise? Das ist aber eine tolle Idee! Kredite kann schließlich jeder. Und festverzinsliche Wertpapiere sowieso. Aber Gold???!!! Wie heißt's doch gleich: Gold verdirbt nicht! Gold rostet nicht! Gold ist ein zeitloser Wertträger! Und, tja, was soll man sagen - selten dürfte ein deutsches Geldinstitut eine lukrativere Entscheidung getroffen haben als unsere mittelgroße Sparkasse, die irgendwann anfing, in Schweizer Tresoren riesige Goldbestände anzuhäufen. Mit dem ETF Rürup von Raisin investieren Sie breit gestreut und kostengünstig in Aktien- und Anleihen-ETFs und können in 2025 bis zu 29.344 € steuerlich geltend machen. Für Ehepaare gilt der doppelte Betrag. Wenn Sie sich den Steuervorteil für 2025 noch sichern wollen, muss das Produkt bis zum 12. Dezember 2025 abgeschlossen werden. Jetzt sichern.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=a48a03336d&e=8f69674dd2> Von HCOB bis HVB - diese Banken haben ein Cum-Cum-Problem (frei zugänglich) Vieles liegt immer noch im Dunkeln bei "Cum-Cum" - eines aber weiß man: Insgesamt 54 deutsche Banken haben sich erklärtermaßen an den umstrittenen Aktiengeschäften beteiligt (überwiegend in den später Nuller- und frühen 2010er-Jahren). Und zumindest für einige von ihnen könnten die alten Steuer-Deals jetzt richtig teuer werden. Zum Beispiel für die Deka, die in vorauseilendem Gehorsam inzwischen fast 500 Mio. Euro an den Fiskus überwiesen hat, wie Finanz-Szene aufdeckte<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=85b581d489&e=8f69674dd2>. Oder für die hiesige Tochter der schwedischen SEB Bank, deren Zwischenrechnung sogar rund viermal so hoch ausfällt<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=33094ee0a0&e=8f69674dd2>. Und wie ist es bei den anderen??? (Bei den besagten 54 Instituten handelt es sich übrigens um 19 öffentliche, 15 genossenschaftliche und 20 private Banken; auch das geht aus der zugrundeliegenden Bafin-Umfrage hervor, die schon 2021 erhoben, allerdings erst Ende 2024 durch eine Anfrage der "Linken" öffentlich gemacht wurde). Fest steht: Der Druck steigt. Seit die Bundesregierung die Finanzverwaltungen im Jahr 2021 anwies, die Cum-Cum-Deals kritischer unter die Lupe zu nehmen<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=e1ededf8a9&e=8f69674dd2>, sehen sich Banken und Sparkassen immer öfter mit entsprechenden Steuernachforderungen konfrontiert. Auch darüber hinaus kommt Bewegung in die Sache. So ließ ein Gericht erstmals überhaupt ein Strafverfahren in Zusammenhang mit Cum-Cum-Gestaltungen zu. Die hessische Steuerverwaltung tönt derweil selbstbewusst, die alten Cum-Cum-Geschäfte mithilfe neuester KI durchleuchten zu wollen. Und während der neue Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil die Aufbewahrungsfrist für Steuerbelege nun doch wieder auf zehn Jahre ausgedehnt hat (was direkte Auswirkungen auf Cum-Cum hat), warb in Nordrhein-Westfalen die Finanzverwaltung offensiv: "Cum-Cum-Fahnder gesucht!" Kochen demnächst also noch mehr hoch? Und bei wie vielen der insgesamt 54 Banken weiß man überhaupt, um wen es sich handelt? content: From: Maier, Lisa (C&I) <Lisa.Maier@natwestmarkets.com> Sent: Tuesday, November 11, 2025 4:56 PM To: Eschwege, Felix (C&I) <felix.eschwege@natwestmarkets.com> Cc: Weiss, Daniel (C&I) <Daniel.Weiss@natwestmarkets.com>; Maier, Lisa (C&I) <Lisa.Maier@natwestmarkets.com> Subject: NatWest Markets - Rates Update | 11/11/2025 Hi All, It was a busy week for G3 swap rates. Notably, GBP swap rates rallied (i.e., bond yields down, prices up) following the MPC meeting on Thursday as Governor Bailey hinted towards further easing as early as December should disinflation prove to be durable given upcoming data releases. USD swap rates experienced mid-week volatility - strong ADP employment data initially suggested labour market resilience, but this was later offset by a sharp rise in October layoffs reported in the Challenger Job Cuts release on Thursday. Additionally, the Fed's Barr noted ongoing progress in bringing inflation under control later on in the day. For more detailed commentary on economic outlook and rates, please find our Strategy Team's Weekly Corporate Treasurer Letter here<https://marketinsights.natwest.com/s/shared-article?a=VGQwMDAwMDBCM1lySUFL>. Latest market updates can be found on our Market Insights Page here<https://marketinsights.natwest.com/s/>. GBP Update * It was a moderate week for GBP swap rates which closed c.3 bps up overall. The main event of the week saw swap rates rally c.5 bps on Thursday following the MPC meeting which saw the BoE hold interest rates at 4.00% as was widely anticipated, but a 5-4 vote outcome and softer tone on inflation gave the decision an overall dovish lean. Governor Bailey signalled openness to easing if disinflation proves to be durable, although emphasised the need for confirmation in upcoming data releases. As a result, market participants increased their expectation of a year-end 25 bp cut from c.38% to c.71% probability following the MPC meeting. * Our Strategists have revised their BoE Base Rate forecast expecting just one further 25bp cut to a 3.75% terminal rate to be delivered in February 2026, although they do note that probability of a December cut has increased. The market is pricing in c.22 bps rate cuts for the rest of the year. * Highlights of the week include: * UK Unemployment and PAYE Payrolls (today): UK Unemployment for September printed at 5.0% (vs. 4.9% market consensus forecast, vs. 4.8% prior) and PAYE Payrolls came in lower than expect at -32k (vs. -3k market consensus forecast, vs. -32k prior). * UK GDP QoQ and YoY (Thursday): GDP is expected to come in at +0.2% QoQ (vs. +0.3% prior) and +1.4% YoY (in-line with prior). * UK Industrial and Manufacturing Production (Thursday): September's Industrial Production is expected to come in at -0.2% MoM (vs. +0.4% prior) and Manufacturing Production is expected to come in at -0.3% MoM (vs. +0.7% prior). * Currently, 2yr, 5yr, and 10yr GBP swap rates vs. SONIA are trading at 3.50%, 3.57%, and 3.89%, respectively. Mid-Market Screen Swap Rates vs. SONIA Source: NWM/Bloomberg [cid:image001.png@01DC532B.78E93200] EUR Update * It was another quiet week for EUR swap rates which closed c.1 bps up overall. The main event of the week was EUR swap rates selling off c.2 bps due to supply and demand dynamics as France issued a series of short-dated bills pushing yields up and prices down. * The ECB is expected to keep rates on hold at 2%, which our Strategists continue to view as terminal for this cycle with no trigger for another cut on the back of recent data releases. Currently, the market is pricing in c.1 bps rate cuts for the rest of the year. * It is a relatively quiet week on the economic calendar, with highlights including: * EA Industrial Production (Thursday): September's production is expect to come in at +0.7% MoM (vs. -1.2% prior) and +2.1% YoY (vs. 1.1% prior). * EA GDP (Friday): GDP is expected to grow +0.2% QoQ (in-line with prior) and +1.3% YoY (in-line with prior). * Currently, 2yr, 5yr, and 10yr EUR swap rates vs. 3m EURIBOR are trading at 2.06%, 2.29%, and 2.62%, respectively Mid-Market Screen Swap Rates vs. 3m EURIBOR Source: NWM/Bloomberg [cid:image003.png@01DC53EE.DF11A670] USD Update * USD swap rates closed c.2 bps down overall despite experiencing volatility mid-week. The main event was a c.7 bps sell-off on Wednesday following the release of the ADP employment report which showed private sector jobs increased by +42k (vs. 30k consensus forecast, vs. -29k prior) in October, suggesting a strengthening labour market. Given the Fed's recent shift in policy and a December not guaranteed, this release was interpreted as an early indication for a hold on rates at the upcoming FOMC December meeting. Our Strategists do caution that despite the ADP data being the market's leading employment indicator given the absence of NFP prints amid the US government shutdown, its accuracy varies month on month and should be interpreted carefully. * Thursday opened with a c.3 bps rally early in the morning as Challenger Job Cuts came in at +175.3% (vs. -25.8%), suggesting a surge in layoffs over the month of October reversing the previous days momentum. The rally was sustained as Fed's Barr gave a positive speech stating that progress has been made on inflation despite still more “work to do”, driving swap rates down further by c.6 bps through the day. Market participants reassessed their expectation of a rate cut at the December FOMC meeting, increasing their view of a 25 bp cut from c.62% to c.72% probability by the end of the session. * Following the Fed's cut last week and despite the revised stance on a December cut, our Strategists still back a further 25 bp to be delivered next month. Our Strategists are also adding in an additional 75bps of easing post-Powell's term into their forecast profile (expectation of a 50bp cut in June and a 25bp cut in July). Currently, the market is pricing in c.17 bps rate cuts for the rest of the year. * It is expected to be a quiet week for data releases given the ongoing US Government shutdown, with the highlight of the week including: * US Core CPI (Thursday): October's Core CPI is expected to come in at +0.3% MoM (vs. +0.2% prior) and +3.0 YoY (in-line with prior). * Currently, 2yr, 5yr, and 10yr USD swap rates vs SOFR are trading at 3.35%, 3.41%, 3.68%, respectively. Mid-Market Screen Swap Rates vs. SOFR Source: NWM/Bloomberg [cid:image004.png@01DC532B.78E93200] All of our Strategy team's output is available through our Market Insights platform, from which you can receive all of our forecasts and updates (including our daily Morning Call email). We also produce a couple of podcasts towards the end of each week “Bondcast” and the “Currency Exchange”. These are particularly useful for a high level overview of what's driving rates markets so do hit subscribe in Apple Music or Spotify to get the latest episodes. Im Browser lesen<https://view.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=d174afae07bd2d12a6c96bae278dfd367ca69e32bf9b6a2bd7cc13835f783abdb3297bd6d0270557ba677f89627efab44dd0d2c900bf9be96f6ddf5c399ec84aaff1acc4e62e2c30b41728840e11a3da>

Das Wichtigste aus der Wirtschaft
­
[https://cdn.prod.www.manager-magazin.de/images/21092977-f22b-407e-af93-e3bdef727e76_w112_r1_fpx48_fpy52.jpg]
Claudia Witte
Redakteurin manager magazin
Lieber Herr Frignani.

Wenn Sie auswärts essen gehen, ist die Wahrscheinlichkeit hoch, dass an der Zubereitung Ihres Gerichts ein Gerät der Rational AG aus dem bayerischen Landsberg am Lech beteiligt ist. Rational ist Weltmarktführer für moderne Profi-Küchengeräte, mit seinen Maschinen werden Gourmetdinner in Hilton-Hotels ebenso zubereitet wie Köttbullar bei Ikea oder die Bordverpflegung bei Singapore Airlines.

Anlagen wie der Kombidämpfer können nicht nur kochen, backen, braten und dünsten, sie sind auch vernetzt und lassen sich zentral überwachen. Der Betreiber oder Rational selbst spielen Rezepte direkt auf die smarten Maschinen, die dank Garintelligenz immer selbstständiger werden: Anbrennen, Zerkochen, Überlaufen  ausgeschlossen. Auch unterschiedliche Kochkulturen lassen sich einstellen: Bei der Systemsprache Französisch wird das Gemüse automatisch bissfester, bei Englisch werden die Steaks blutiger. Unser Autor Claus Gorgs nimmt Sie mit in die Großküche und zeigt Ihnen, wie Rational das Kochen revolutioniert und nebenbei den Fachkräftemangel eindampft: Es ist angerichtet. (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a59578d7bb5781b70d12d8dd01ecaa2cea6dfab34bfa681e7cd5c085d792de2f6fd417ecd7ee40cdc64c3c1351af984e669758980aa40e3cbd79>

Niete am Herd mit Erfolgsrezept: Vorstandschef Peter Stadelmann hat aus dem Großküchenausrüster Rational ein Milliardenunternehmen gemacht. Kochen kann er selbst aber nicht.

Thomas Dashuber / laif

[separator]
Die Wirtschaftsnews des Tages:

  *   Aus dem Bieterwettkampf um den Anti-Adipositas-Spezialisten Metsera geht der US-Pharmariese Pfizer als Gewinner hervor<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a595da2cecc6052d782e6f44245f51c23967edc07c1e494d828ba7f334843085bc4ea0fd02500293377f875c64bb6ba05e62c9c0f34c4d639023>. Der unterlegene Rivale Novo Nordisk hatte gehofft, durch den Zukauf seine Position im Wettbewerb der Abnehmspritzen zu stärken.

  *   Der deutsche Cloud-Anbieter Northern Data geht an Rumble<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a59577f6189307536369e6c1e45ca709133cccf716f096bdf02cdbf09922d7ab140a904ab4ee648e46e81af316125475c0d40d40c5769cc2b76c>. Die US-Firma betreibt die gleichnamige, bei rechten Influencern beliebte Videoplattform und zudem die Cloud von Truth Social, dem Kurzmitteilungsdienst von US-Präsident Donald Trump (79).

  *   Heute hat die Weltklimakonferenz in Brasilien begonnen. Wir stellen die Knackpunkte<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a59568d95b04d4e8f224a9114e9ae289d503e2427d5b5d0f6fbae3988f9a5593f260781d5eaea1e18c3727cc16429cdcf3cec24e5c0d79db0c8d> vor.

[separator]
Was uns heute besonders beschäftigt hat:

  *   Patricia Schlesinger (64) machte in ihrer Zeit als Intendantin des Rundfunk Berlin-Brandenburg (RBB) Schlagzeilen mit Vorwürfen der Verschwendung und Vetternwirtschaft, die sie den Job kosteten. Es ging um teure Dienstwagen, Essen auf Senderkosten, Dienstreisen, Zulagen für Führungskräfte und um ein inzwischen eingestampftes Millionen-Bauprojekt. Wie tritt die einst mächtige Medienfrau in ihrer neuen Rolle bei der kleinen Berliner Agentur Stella auf, wo sie fortan Führungskräfte coachen will? Jedenfalls nicht in der Rolle der Gescheiterten (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a595871b9e68011b6c4a408b094f7ea08f3af696cafa9e479b5b683fe037034d9fadb8c0d05c2c5ddf982e80c570dbfe941667f9f41e0139a61a>, hat mein Kollege Henning Hinze beobachtet.

[separator]
Was Ihnen in Ihrem Team weiterhelfen könnte:

  *   Untersuchungen des Beratungsunternehmens McKinsey zeigen, dass bis zu 45 Prozent der Leistungsschwankungen eines Unternehmens direkt mit der Effektivität des CEOs zusammenhängen. Und wenn der Chef eine Niete ist? Wie Sie Ihr Team schützen, die Geschäfte steuern und dabei den Chef in Schach halten, erfahren Sie hier: Fünf Strategien für die Praxis. (HBm+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a5956525b998c118188f5f082e4be12030e842ae446f3aa514ef4539e69de3c59317dc9398a2faab2469d7de38286455c2844af21b6f2ca00c03>

[separator]
Meine Empfehlung für den Abend:
[Der Arzt, der glaubt, als Unternehmer mehr Menschen helfen zu können: Futrue-Gründer Clemens Fischer]

Der Arzt, der glaubt, als Unternehmer mehr Menschen helfen zu können: Futrue-Gründer Clemens Fischer

Sandra Singh / manager magazin

  *   Heute können wir Sie mit einer großen Portion Hoffnung in den Feierabend entlassen: Der Arzt und Unternehmer Clemens Fischer (50) will mit einer Hanfarznei die Welt von chronischen Schmerzen erlösen. Fischer ist in der Pharmawelt kein Unbekannter, mit seiner Firma Futrue hat ihn das Beratungsunternehmen EY gerade in der Kategorie Innovation zum Entrepreneur des Jahres 2025<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a595e9476bfd3abc68e72c0863a8269a2bcd5b7c8f592fe0d21a1bd0099f2cc9e4185baf320d5613fc6e00a17e9e59c80bbbc2681e2125d9b3a6> gekürt. Reich wurde er mit einem Imperium frei verkäuflicher Medikamente wie dem Reizdarmpräparat Kijimea. So brachte er es bis auf Platz 340 in unserer Liste der 500 reichsten Deutschen (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a595abb380ffb44e837486d87c0e8f6b2b990c1e099faaba3af093ddb152998e6c6e163e5c44508cb7bc6b25e778ad2ed17726d723be9174cf24>. Mein Kollege Stefan Merx hat dem visionären Unternehmer den Puls gefühlt (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=f9c9877c6404a5950b6525681c0454c335c3428d472a4383f355a417228014418ad7111c4b61588f7a64a93310ecd000d86b487e9ec797b5f3631f8b188a56a0>.

Ich wünsche Ihnen einen schönen Abend
Ihre Claudia Witte
